Part 1 · Booking a community kitchen

Coordinator: Good afternoon, Riverside Community Kitchen. How can I help?
Caller: Our neighbourhood group wants to run a cooking evening. We used the church hall last year, but it had only two small ovens, and people spent more time waiting than cooking. Someone said your kitchen could accommodate twelve people working together.
Coordinator: Twelve is our maximum for a practical class. We can seat more for a demonstration, but that doesn’t sound like your plan. Will one person be responsible for the booking?
Caller: Yes, that will be me, Anna Mercer. I sometimes get letters addressed to Merker, but it’s Mercer, M-E-R-C-E-R. The group itself is called Shared Table.
Coordinator: Thank you. Were you thinking of a weekday evening or a weekend? Saturday afternoons are mostly reserved for our own courses, although there’s one gap later this month.
Caller: We first discussed Friday, but two members finish work late then. Thursday is the day we’ve agreed on. We’d prefer the second week of next month if that’s available.
Coordinator: It is. You could have the room from six, but another group finishes just before that. If you want it fully reset before you arrive, I’d recommend six thirty. Would that leave enough time?
Caller: Yes, let’s start at 6:30. We can circulate recipes beforehand rather than spend the first half-hour explaining them. Is there a minimum hire period?
Coordinator: Three hours. The charge for a community group is eighteen pounds an hour. Businesses pay twenty-five, but your event qualifies for the lower rate, so the hire will be fifty-four pounds. Cleaning is included if you leave the work surfaces clear.
Caller: That’s manageable. Do we pay the whole amount now?
Coordinator: No, a deposit of twenty pounds confirms it. The balance is due one week beforehand. We send a reminder, but please don’t depend on receiving it if your email changes.
---
Caller: We’ll be making vegetable dishes. Is there anything we should bring besides ingredients? Our organiser has a set of knives, though carrying them across town seems unnecessary.
Coordinator: Knives and boards are supplied, and so are pans. Every participant needs an apron. We used to lend those, but laundering them was becoming difficult. Ordinary comfortable clothes and enclosed shoes are sensible too.
Caller: One member uses a wheelchair. I saw a photograph of steps at the front. Is there another way in?
Coordinator: Yes. The side entrance is level and opens directly into the kitchen corridor. The front doors are mainly used for the meeting rooms. I’ll include a little plan in the confirmation so nobody has to search after dark.
Caller: That would help. Can we store ingredients before the event? A couple of people can deliver things during their lunch break, but nobody wants to leave milk in an office all afternoon.
Coordinator: You can use the fridge from midday on the day. Label everything with your group’s name, please. The freezer is already allocated to our regular classes, so don’t bring anything that requires freezing.
Caller: Fine. What do you need from me to finish the booking?
Coordinator: A contact number and a copy of your proposed menu. We don’t approve individual recipes, but we need to know about activities requiring unusual equipment. Email the menu by Monday, and we’ll confirm any questions before you buy ingredients.
Caller: I’ll send it this weekend. Where should we meet our participants?
Coordinator: The easiest landmark is the library opposite us. Ask everyone to wait there rather than beside the narrow driveway. You can collect the group together and use the side entrance. I’ll arrange for someone to show you the controls when you arrive.

Part 2 · Welcome to the riverside craft fair

Host: Welcome to our annual riverside craft fair. Before you explore, I’ll explain the site and mention a few changes to the programme. Please keep the printed plan facing the way you entered: the gate is at the bottom and the river at the top. The main path runs straight from the gate towards the river. The letters on the plan mark places, not the names of activities. We have kept the central crossing clear so visitors can move between the two sides without walking through a stall queue.
The information tent is the first place on your left as you come through the gate. You can leave a message there if you become separated from someone. Directly opposite it, on the right-hand side of the entrance path, is the bag store. Please don’t confuse the two. We can keep a coat or shopping bag in the store, but valuables should stay with you. There is no charge, though everything must be collected before we close.
Continue up the path to the crossing. The pottery demonstrations are on the left, in the middle row of the plan. The demonstrators need water, which is why they aren’t using the dry space near the gate this year. Across the path in the same row is the repair stall. Bring a small household object there and the volunteers will discuss what might be possible. They cannot promise to complete every repair during the fair, but can often identify the next useful step.
At the far end, beside the river, you’ll find the quiet seating area. It’s the space on the left, not the performance platform on the right. We’ve kept music away from that seating because some visitors want somewhere to rest and talk without raising their voices. The central space nearest the river is being kept empty for access, and it isn’t an extra picnic area.
---
Now, about today’s arrangements. The fair has been moved from Sunday to Saturday this year because the riverside road will be used for a running event tomorrow. It wasn’t a change caused by the weather forecast, and it has nothing to do with the availability of the makers. Most have reserved both dates anyway. We hope announcing it early has prevented wasted journeys.
There will be a small admission charge for the evening music, but entrance to the craft fair itself is free. The money from the music will pay for next year’s sign-language interpretation. We had considered buying more display tables, but accessibility support was the priority chosen at our last public meeting.
For children, there is a short weaving workshop. Parents sometimes expect to leave children there while they shop. This time an adult must stay with each child, since the activity is designed for them to work together. You don’t need to reserve, but if a table is full you’ll be asked to return at the next starting time rather than stand in the working area.
We ask stallholders to avoid disposable packaging where possible. Visitors can help by bringing containers for small purchases. There is a recycling point near the gate, but using fewer packages is our first aim; the recycling bins aren’t a reason to wrap everything twice. Some delicate pieces do need protection, and makers will explain the options.
Finally, if you have comments about the fair, please use the short paper form at the information tent. We will post an online survey next week, but today’s form asks about routes and seating while they’re fresh in your mind. There’s no prize draw attached. We want to hear about a difficulty even if the rest of your visit was enjoyable. Thank you, and have a good afternoon.

Part 3 · Planning a study of queue information

Maya: We need to narrow our project before the methods seminar. I liked the idea of studying queues in the campus café, but counting how long people wait sounds like something the manager could do without us.
Leo: The tutor’s comment was that our original question was too broad. We were trying to measure satisfaction, purchasing and staff performance all at once. Why don’t we focus on whether information changes people’s experience of waiting?
Maya: Like displaying an estimated wait? We shouldn’t promise that information always makes people happier. If the estimate is wrong, it could make things worse.
Leo: Exactly. We could compare a simple expected-wait sign with the ordinary queue. But I don’t think asking people to recall the time afterwards gives us a reliable actual duration.
Maya: Let’s have an observer note arrival and service times. Then the questionnaire can ask about perceived waiting, which is a different thing. That distinction might be the useful part of the project.
Leo: We also need comparable periods. Monday lunchtime and Friday afternoon would differ for too many reasons. The manager says the same lunch menu is served on Tuesday and Thursday, and the usual staffing level is the same.
Maya: That’s better, though a club event could still change the crowd. We should log unusual events rather than assuming two days are identical. Maybe use several weeks so that one odd day doesn’t dominate.
Leo: How do we decide who sees the sign? We can’t put it up for one person and hide it from the next if they’re standing together.
Maya: No. Use whole time blocks, alternating the order across days. Otherwise the sign condition would always be later, when perhaps people are less rushed. We need the schedule written before we see any results.
Leo: And the questionnaire must be optional. People are trying to buy lunch, not volunteering for a long interview. A brief invitation after they’ve been served would interfere less than asking while they’re choosing food.
---
Maya: Let’s allocate the preparation. First, the consent notice. I can draft it, but the tutor needs to check the wording. It’s not ready for customers until we have that approval.
Leo: Agreed. The manager’s permission is already sorted. She signed the email yesterday, including the observation positions. We’ll put that in the project folder as completed rather than spend another meeting rewriting it.
Maya: What about the timing sheet? We’ve designed columns, but we haven’t tried using it while several people arrive together. That’s the thing we should pilot before the main collection.
Leo: Yes. We can practise during a quiet half-hour with volunteers, without treating those entries as study data. If we can’t keep track, the form needs changing, not the customers.
Maya: The question about how much money people spend seems unnecessary now. It belonged to the earlier project, and collecting it would make the survey longer without answering our revised question.
Leo: Let’s remove it. We don’t need personal spending information merely because it might be interesting later. The fewer irrelevant details we ask for, the easier it is to explain the purpose honestly.
Maya: We also need a final chart. I started choosing colours, then realised we don’t know the distribution of the data. We could decide what variables belong on it, but should leave the exact display until after collection.
Leo: Right. Averages might hide a few very long waits. We should show enough detail to make those visible, though we don’t need to decide between every possible graph this afternoon.
Maya: I’m glad we narrowed it. The study won’t tell the manager how to redesign the whole café, but it could show whether estimated-wait information changes perceptions under these conditions.
Leo: And if actual times differ between conditions, we’ll report that rather than attribute every difference to the sign. A small honest study is more useful than a grand conclusion our design can’t support.

Part 4 · How wetlands preserve traces of the past

Lecturer: Today we’ll consider why some wetlands contain remarkable archaeological remains, and why discovering those remains creates a new set of problems. When people imagine an ancient object surviving for centuries, they often think of stone or metal. In waterlogged settings, materials such as wood can sometimes remain where they would ordinarily decay. The important condition is not simply that the object is wet. Water can restrict the supply of oxygen, slowing some of the processes that normally destroy organic material. Conditions vary, so the presence of a wetland is not a guarantee that everything deposited there will survive.
Wetland deposits can also build up in layers. A boat landing, a discarded tool and later plant remains may occupy different levels. Archaeologists record these layers because position helps establish relationships between events. A beautiful object removed without its context can answer fewer questions than a less spectacular object whose location was carefully documented. For that reason, a discovery reported promptly by a walker or landowner can be especially valuable. The object may need to be left in place until its surroundings have been recorded and a suitable recovery plan has been made.
One source of evidence is pollen. These tiny particles can survive in certain deposits, and their forms can indicate groups of plants that were present in the surrounding landscape. This does not produce a perfectly detailed picture of an ancient garden. Wind carries some pollen farther than others, and different plants produce different quantities. Researchers therefore compare patterns and use several sources of evidence. A change in pollen may suggest a change in vegetation, but deciding whether people, climate or another process caused it requires additional argument.
Small samples are often examined under a microscope. The work involves identification, counting and attention to possible contamination from more recent material. Sample containers must be labelled clearly, and the sampling position must be recorded. Without that information, laboratory precision cannot restore a lost connection to the site. Researchers may also examine seeds, insects and pieces of wood. Agreement between these sources can strengthen an interpretation, while disagreement can reveal a question that would remain invisible if only one kind of material were studied.
A particularly important threat is drainage. Lowering the water level can expose deposits to air and alter conditions that had preserved them. Damage may begin before a buried structure becomes visible at the surface. Farmers, engineers and archaeologists consequently need ways to exchange information before major ground changes occur. This is not a demand to prohibit every use of wet land. It is an argument for assessing what may be lost while there is still time to modify a plan or record vulnerable evidence properly.
Recovery itself also changes the environment of an object. A wooden implement that looks solid in the ground may distort or crack if it is allowed to dry without treatment. Conservators must plan stabilisation before excavation, including suitable packaging and access to facilities. Removing an object first and searching for money afterwards can leave an institution responsible for material it cannot care for. Sometimes leaving a deposit undisturbed, with monitoring, is the more responsible choice. Excavation is one method of research rather than an automatic reward for every promising discovery.
Finally, consider public interpretation. Museums often display the surviving object but not the months of recording and treatment around it. A useful display can include a reconstruction, provided visitors can distinguish it from the original material. The distinction matters because a completed shape may contain informed guesses. Good interpretation makes those guesses visible without making the object uninteresting. Wetlands preserve opportunities to ask questions about the past. The purpose of careful archaeology is to keep those opportunities connected to evidence rather than turn a fragile discovery into an attractive object stripped of its story.

passages.title: Reading passage 1 · The second life of a railway station
passages.text:
A. When the last passenger train left Mereford's station, the council inherited a building that seemed inconvenient in almost every respect. Its long waiting room was costly to heat, the platform divided the site, and there was little parking. Several councillors favoured demolition. Residents, however, remembered the station as the town's informal meeting place, not merely somewhere to board a train. A public consultation therefore asked what activities the town lacked before asking what should happen to the building. This reversed the usual sequence of choosing a use and then seeking support for it.

B. The consultation revealed demand for spaces that could be borrowed briefly: a room for a job interview, a table for a small club, or somewhere to mend a torn coat. It did not reveal much enthusiasm for another exhibition about railway history. The architects initially proposed one large open hall, believing that maximum flexibility required minimum division. During a trial weekend, however, a children's storytelling session overwhelmed a conversation group at the opposite end. Curtains softened the appearance but did little to stop sound. The final plan included several enclosed rooms with glazed doors, retaining visual openness while allowing incompatible activities to coexist.

C. Keeping the platform was another disputed decision. It could not provide step-free access by itself, and early sketches treated it as an obstacle to be removed. A resident who used a wheelchair suggested a gently sloping route along the outer wall instead. The resulting ramp joined the old platform at its far end and created a sheltered place to wait. It was longer than a direct staircase but required no lift or electrical machinery. The design team subsequently used this route as the principal entrance for everyone, rather than labelling it as a separate accessible entrance.

D. Finances shaped the refurbishment as much as architectural preference. The project had received a grant for construction but no permanent promise to cover running costs. The committee rejected polished stone flooring because its price would consume money needed for insulation. Original floorboards were repaired where possible; damaged sections were replaced with matching reclaimed timber. The choices were not presented as historical reconstruction. The committee wanted a building that could survive everyday wear and remain affordable to maintain, even when the initial excitement had faded and volunteers had other demands on their time.

E. The first winter tested those priorities. A new booking system showed that most daytime users needed only two of the rooms. Heating the entire building for them made little sense, so separate heating controls were installed. Users could reserve adjoining rooms when they needed more space. Electricity use fell, although the committee warned that the mild winter prevented a fair comparison with the station's previous bills. It published monthly meter readings alongside opening hours, allowing residents to see both the expenditure and the amount of activity it supported. No claim of a precise percentage saving was made.

F. Running the centre also required rules that were less visible than the renovation. Small groups could book ordinary meetings without charge, while commercial courses paid a modest fee. A refundable deposit covered the keys, but the committee offered an alternative arrangement for residents who could not afford it. Volunteers discovered that a complicated application form discouraged the very informal groups the centre hoped to attract. They replaced it with a short conversation and a one-page agreement. Insurance and safety requirements remained, but the process no longer assumed that every group had an experienced secretary.

G. After two years, attendance alone was no longer considered a sufficient measure of success. A crowded craft market might attract many people who never returned, while a weekly reading group could matter greatly to six regular participants. The coordinator began keeping a diary of requests that the centre could not accommodate. Some concerned opening hours, others the lack of storage or difficulty reaching the station after the evening bus stopped. This record described unmet needs rather than only celebrating completed bookings. It also helped distinguish problems within the committee's control from those requiring transport or other public services.

H. Mereford's experience offers no simple formula for every disused station. The building benefited from committed residents and a central location, advantages that cannot be manufactured by a clever floor plan. Nevertheless, its history challenges the idea that preserving a public building means preserving its former purpose. Railway objects occupy one small cabinet, while most rooms serve activities never imagined by the original builders. The committee argues that continued usefulness is a stronger defence against neglect than admiration alone. For this station, keeping the building has depended on allowing its social meaning to change.

passages.title: Reading passage 2 · Listening to a landscape
passages.text:
A. A landscape can be surveyed with a camera, but photographs omit much of what happens beyond the visible frame. A recorder left beside a pond may capture insects, traffic, wind and human voices throughout the night. Researchers use the term soundscape for this combined acoustic environment. It is tempting to describe a rich recording as evidence of a healthy ecosystem. Yet an impressive chorus is not a census. A single loud animal can dominate a microphone, while numerous quiet species remain inaudible. The attraction of sound recording lies partly in its reach, but its limitations begin with the same property.

B. In an imagined monitoring project at Bellwater Reserve, ecologist Mara Sen placed identical recorders at twelve ponds. Her colleague, technician Owen Price, suggested positioning them where volunteers could reach them easily. Sen objected that convenient paths might also be the noisiest places. They eventually selected positions using a grid, then documented exceptions where water or private land prevented installation. Each microphone was mounted at the same height. This did not eliminate all environmental differences, but it made the reasons for variation more visible. A comparable procedure mattered more than locating the most spectacular sounds.

C. The team soon encountered a less obvious problem: rain striking protective covers sounded remarkably like repeated animal calls to an automatic detector. Price redesigned the cover and added a short record of weather conditions to every file. Simply deleting all wet nights would have introduced a different bias, because some animals are especially active after rainfall. Instead, the team labelled intervals in which rain interfered with identification. A recording could therefore remain in the archive without being treated as reliable evidence for every possible question. Quality was attached to particular uses, not to the file as a whole.

D. For comparison with the machine, volunteers listened to short extracts and marked calls they recognised. Training began with clear examples, but Sen insisted on including ambiguous ones before volunteers worked independently. She wanted listeners to recognise uncertainty, not merely memorise ideal calls. Each extract was assessed by two people who could not see one another's decisions. Disagreements were retained for review rather than resolved by automatically choosing the more confident listener. Confidence, Sen noted, was itself a human judgement; it could reflect familiarity with a training example rather than a genuinely distinctive sound.

E. Software made it possible to search months of recordings quickly. However, detector developer Lila Tran warned against comparing a new system only with its own earlier version. If both versions missed the same quiet species, an apparent improvement could still leave a major gap. Her team built a separate reference set, including recordings from sites absent from the training collection. Performance fell on these unfamiliar sites. Tran regarded this as useful information about the limits of transfer, although a sponsor had hoped to advertise a single accuracy figure. A lower, properly qualified result could guide deployment more effectively than an impressive average.

F. Interpreting changes over time required another distinction. A decline in detected calls might mean fewer animals, but it could also mean that traffic had increased, masking the same population. Sen therefore paired acoustic observations with occasional visual surveys. These surveys were expensive and covered shorter periods, yet they offered a different kind of evidence. When the two sources disagreed, the team investigated rather than discarding the inconvenient result. No instrument acted as a final judge. The purpose of combining methods was to expose their different blind spots, not to declare that agreement was guaranteed.

G. The recordings also contained conversations from a footpath near two ponds. Local adviser Imani Cole argued that obtaining permission to place a recorder was not the same as obtaining permission to distribute everything it captured. The public archive consequently excluded speech-containing segments, while authorised researchers could request restricted access for an approved purpose. This reduced the amount of openly available material. Cole considered the restriction a condition of responsible monitoring rather than a failure of scientific openness. Signs near the path explained what was collected and whom residents could contact, including people who never used the project's website.

H. Soundscape research thus involves more than replacing field visits with unattended devices. Decisions about placement, weather, training and access shape the evidence long before anyone draws an ecological conclusion. Bellwater's fictional project illustrates why cheap data collection need not produce cheap interpretation. The recorder can work while a researcher sleeps, but it cannot decide which uncertainty matters or whose privacy deserves attention. For Sen, the most valuable outcome was not a claim that every pond had been understood. It was a record detailed enough for later researchers to ask different questions without mistaking the original team's choices for facts about nature.

passages.title: Reading passage 3 · The value of leaving room to choose
passages.text:
A. The promise of a recommendation system is that it will make an excessive range of choices manageable. A reader opens a catalogue and receives a short list rather than confronting thousands of titles. At its best, such help makes unfamiliar material accessible. Yet a catalogue is also an environment in which preferences develop. A system that repeatedly supplies what someone already appears to like can quietly decide which alternatives the person ever encounters. The central question is therefore not whether recommendations are accurate, but what kind of opportunity that accuracy creates or removes.

B. One account of good recommendation treats a successful click as evidence that a person's desire has been satisfied. This is reasonable for a narrow request: someone looking for a particular manual benefits from finding it quickly. But a click on an unexpected article may mean curiosity, irritation or accidental selection. Even a long reading time is ambiguous when the text is unusually difficult. Behavioural traces are useful evidence, not transparent windows into intention. A designer who calls every measurable response a revealed preference risks turning the convenience of measurement into a theory of human motivation.

C. Consider a fictional community library that experiments with two digital shelves. The first orders books by predicted borrowing probability. The second includes a small space for titles selected to differ from the reader's recent loans. During the trial, the second shelf produces fewer immediate reservations but more reports of discovering an unfamiliar author. Neither result alone settles which shelf is better. A reservation and a discovery describe different benefits, and discovery itself may take weeks to become a borrowing decision. Judging the trial by the fastest observable response would build the desired conclusion into the measurement.

D. Advocates of prediction sometimes reply that users can simply leave the recommended shelf. Formally, the rest of the catalogue is available. Practically, the cost of reaching it matters. A link hidden below several screens is a weaker invitation than a prominent search box. This does not mean every arrangement is manipulation; all interfaces distribute attention in some way. It means that an assessment of freedom must consider effort as well as formal availability. A choice can remain technically possible while becoming unlikely enough to disappear from most people's ordinary experience.

E. There is an opposing danger in praising surprise without qualification. A system that inserts unfamiliar items arbitrarily may waste time and undermine trust. The relevant distinction is between useful exploration and mere randomness. Someone learning a language might welcome material slightly beyond their current interests, provided its difficulty remains manageable. The same person may not welcome an unrelated technical document presented as an exciting discovery. Good exploration needs a relationship to the user's purpose, even when it challenges a narrow prediction of their taste. Difference is a means to an opportunity, not an achievement by itself.

F. Giving users control can help, but control must be intelligible. A panel containing many unexplained settings transfers work without necessarily transferring power. More useful controls might let a reader request greater variety, inspect why an item appeared, or temporarily ignore earlier borrowing history. Explanations need not expose every mathematical operation. They should reveal the practical basis of a suggestion well enough for a person to dispute it. If a system infers an interest from a book borrowed for somebody else, the user needs a simple way to correct the inference rather than a technical lecture about the model.

G. Institutions also need to decide what they will refuse to optimise. A public library may legitimately value access to minority-language material even when predicted demand is low. That choice is not a defect in prediction; it is a statement about the institution's purpose. Leaving such decisions entirely to a model hides a public judgement behind an apparently neutral calculation. Conversely, declaring values does not excuse a badly functioning search service. Institutions need evidence that their systems work and an explicit account of what working means. Technical performance and public responsibility answer different questions, but neither can replace the other.

H. The best recommendation systems may therefore be those that know when to recede. They can help with a defined search, offer a defensible suggestion and then leave a visible route beyond it. This is not a demand that every user spend more time choosing. For some tasks, fewer decisions are a real benefit. It is a demand that efficiency remain answerable to the person's changing purposes. A successful system should reduce unnecessary effort without treating yesterday's pattern as tomorrow's boundary. The aim is assistance that preserves the possibility of becoming interested in something the model did not anticipate.

scripts:
Part 1 · Joining a neighbourhood walking group

Volunteer: Hello, Green Routes walking group. You’re speaking to Max.
Caller: Hello. I’d like to join one of your weekend walks. I saw a leaflet at the health centre, but it listed several groups and I wasn’t sure which one was suitable. I walk to work, though I haven’t done anything long in the countryside recently.
Volunteer: Our introductory route would be a sensible start. It’s mostly level and has places to stop. Could I take your name first? We keep a list so that the leader knows whom to expect, but we don’t ask for medical details on the telephone.
Caller: It’s Joel Ashby. That’s A-S-H-B-Y. My cousin has the same surname with an extra letter, so I usually spell it. Is there an annual membership payment?
Volunteer: There is for the longer programme, but your first walk costs nothing. You can decide about joining afterwards. The next introductory one is on Sunday. We used to run it on Saturday, but the leader now works then.
Caller: Sunday is better for me anyway. Where do you meet? The leaflet mentioned the station.
Volunteer: That was the starting point while the footbridge was being repaired. We’re back at the museum now, beside its main doors. It’s easy to find from the bus stop, and there’s shelter if people arrive early.
Caller: And how early is early? I prefer not to rush off a bus straight into a long walk.
Volunteer: We gather at nine fifteen and leave at nine thirty. Put 9:15 in your diary, because the leader gives a short briefing before departure. If you’re delayed, call the number on the confirmation rather than trying to catch up alone.
Caller: How far will we go? I can manage four kilometres comfortably, but eight might be a bit much the first time.
Volunteer: This one is six kilometres. There’s a shorter return option if someone needs it, although most people complete the full route. We don’t use the speed of the fastest person to set the pace. The leader stays aware of the group and a second volunteer walks at the back.
---
Caller: I own ordinary trainers. Would I need to buy boots before coming?
Volunteer: Not for this route if it’s dry. Trainers with a good grip are fine. Please bring a waterproof, though. A forecast can change, and the riverside section has nowhere to shelter. A large umbrella is awkward on the narrow path, so a jacket is more useful.
Caller: Should I bring lunch as well?
Volunteer: A snack and some water. We finish near a café, but buying anything there is entirely optional. Carry a bottle rather than depending on places along the way, since the public fountain is currently out of use.
Caller: I sometimes use a walking pole. Is the path wide enough for that?
Volunteer: Yes. There’s one section with a stile, but we use a nearby gate instead. We don’t go up the steps shown on an older route map. If you have any concerns about the gate width or surface, the leader can discuss them before the day.
Caller: That sounds reassuring. Can people bring dogs? My neighbour might come, and hers is very calm.
Volunteer: Dogs aren’t permitted on this particular walk because we cross a field containing livestock. Some of our other routes welcome them. It isn’t a general judgement about well-behaved dogs; it’s an agreement with the farmer for this route.
Caller: Fair enough. What happens if there’s severe weather? Would you call everyone?
Volunteer: We send a text by eight that morning if we cancel. For ordinary rain the walk usually goes ahead, but strong wind near the trees is different. Please reply to acknowledge a cancellation so we know you won’t travel unnecessarily. I’ll send a confirmation now with the route description and the leader’s contact number.

Part 2 · An orientation talk at a community arts centre

Director: Welcome to everyone starting a course at the Foundry Arts Centre. The building was once a small factory, but its new name isn’t an invitation to operate industrial equipment. We run practical arts courses for adults, and some family sessions during school holidays. Today I’ll describe five activities you may want to try and then explain how the centre works. You don’t have to decide everything this morning. The aim is to help you understand which course fits the time and experience you actually have.
First, bookbinding. This starts next week and lasts four Tuesday evenings. Materials are provided, but we require a reservation because the tutor prepares a separate pack for each person. Turning up on the first evening and hoping to find an empty chair won’t work, even if someone is absent. We can often offer a place on the next course instead.
The lunchtime sketch group is quite different. There is no advance booking and no expectation that you already draw well. Its special arrangement is that it’s held outside the centre, in the covered market across the road. The group meets under the market clock. This gives people moving subjects to draw, and traders have agreed that participants may sit along the wall without blocking customers.
For textile printing, you should bring something of your own to print on. A plain cotton bag is ideal; a smooth T-shirt is another possibility. We provide inks and tools, but not the fabric item itself. Please avoid a favourite expensive garment for your first experiment. The tutor will explain why different surfaces absorb colour differently.
Our percussion session has been moved to an earlier time. People used to arrive at seven on Wednesdays; it now begins at six, because the neighbouring room is needed for a quiet class later in the evening. That’s a permanent change for this term, not just for the first week.
Finally, the clay modelling course allows children to attend, provided an adult takes the course with them. It isn’t a supervised drop-off club. Both people make something and can help each other. If you were hoping to work completely on your own, choose the adults-only session on the other day.
---
Now for some general information. Membership fees cover the shared studio space and basic maintenance. They don’t cover every course material. We used to charge one inclusive fee, but someone taking only sketching was helping pay for expensive clay. Separating the costs makes the arrangement more transparent, even though the price list is slightly longer.
Our noticeboard displays examples of work, but you don’t have to agree to public display. Some people enjoy sharing a first attempt; others want to practise privately. Ask the tutor to mark your work as not for display. That decision will have no effect on your access to future courses or the amount of help you receive.
Equipment may stay in the studio between sessions, but unfinished pieces must have a name and date. Unlabelled work is difficult to store responsibly because staff can’t tell whether it has been abandoned. We won’t throw things away immediately. After a published storage period, we’ll contact the maker where possible and clear space for current classes.
The café next door offers a small discount to course members on weekday afternoons. It is independent of the centre, so please raise food orders with café staff rather than a tutor. We mention it because many students like to continue talking after class, not because a café purchase is part of membership.
Please tell us if you need adjustments to take part. The best time is when you book, because some arrangements require planning. However, if you discover a difficulty during a session, speak to the tutor then. We don’t expect you to predict every problem in advance. The office can discuss an alternative rather than simply telling you to wait until the next term.

Part 3 · Reviewing an interview project

Tutor: Come in, Amira and Ben. I’ve read your proposal about independent shopkeepers. You’ve found an interesting question about how businesses adapt when a street changes, but I think we need to look closely at recruitment.
Amira: We’ve made a list from the traders' association website. It seemed better than walking along the street and approaching whoever wasn’t busy.
Tutor: It’s organised, certainly. But remember that the association includes only members. Shops that closed recently won’t appear, and new businesses may not have joined. If you use it alone, you’ll hear from a particular surviving group.
Ben: We could add names from older street directories and contact the former owners where details are public. We can’t guarantee they’ll agree, but at least the recruitment frame wouldn’t automatically exclude them.
Amira: Should we ask the association chair to conduct the introductions? People know her, so perhaps they’d speak more freely.
Tutor: She can circulate an invitation. I wouldn’t have her sitting in the interviews. A trader might hesitate to criticise a scheme the association supported. Make clear that the project isn’t a performance review and that individual statements won’t be sent to her.
Ben: Our draft starts with, 'How has the new pedestrian area improved your business?' I can see now that assumes an improvement.
Amira: We should ask what changed, if anything, and then invite positive and negative examples. Otherwise we’d be providing the conclusion in the question.
Tutor: Good. You’ll also need to distinguish memory from records. Someone may recall fewer customers during construction, but sales figures could follow a different pattern. Ask whether records are available without making their participation depend on handing over private accounts.
Ben: We planned an audio recording rather than trying to write everything while they speak. We’d ask permission first and offer a note-only interview if they prefer.
Tutor: That’s sensible. Explain where the file will be kept and when it will be deleted. Permission to talk to you is not permission to put a voice recording on a public website.
---
Amira: We made a checklist of remaining tasks. For the recruitment invitation, we need approval from you before sending it. We’ve drafted it but haven’t contacted anyone yet.
Tutor: Send it after this meeting. The interview schedule is different: its wording needs a trial. Ask somebody outside the final sample to respond, so you can see whether the order makes sense and how long it takes.
Ben: The street map is finished. We’ve marked present businesses and former addresses from the directories, and checked that none of the symbols hides the street names.
Tutor: Fine, treat that as completed for now. Don’t spend another day improving its colours at the expense of preparation.
Amira: We also had a question asking each trader for their exact annual income. It doesn’t answer our revised question and might put people off, so we intend to remove it.
Tutor: I agree. You can ask how they describe changes without collecting an unnecessary financial profile. Remember that an interview isn’t improved merely by making it longer.
Ben: Our coding categories are still provisional. We thought we’d wait until after the first interviews before deciding the final set. We have broad interests, but people may describe problems we haven’t anticipated.
Tutor: Yes, retain that flexibility. Keep a record of changes to the categories, though. You shouldn’t quietly redefine them every time you encounter an inconvenient example.
Amira: Would it be useful to compare two of us coding the same short extract?
Tutor: Very useful, as a way to discuss interpretation rather than produce a ceremonial agreement figure. If you disagree, ask whether the categories are unclear or the account genuinely supports more than one reading. The explanation of that decision may be more valuable than an artificially neat table.

Part 4 · The changing idea of a standard measure

Lecturer: Think about buying a length of cloth from someone you have never met. The transaction requires more than agreement about price. You need a shared understanding of length. Today I’ll discuss standard measures as a social arrangement as well as a technical achievement. A measure is useful when different people can reproduce it closely enough for the task. That does not mean every task needs the same precision. Selling cloth and testing an optical instrument place different demands on the system, even though both involve statements about distance.
Early local arrangements often used a physical reference kept in a public place. Traders could compare their own rods with it. The object represented authority as well as length: somebody had to decide who could inspect it and what happened if a trader’s measure differed. Copies made trading easier, but each copy introduced the possibility of error. Wear, damage and the method of comparison could change the result. The practical problem was not solved simply by declaring that one reference existed. People needed a dependable chain connecting everyday measures to it.
Expansion of trade increased the value of compatibility. Two towns could each have internally consistent measures and still face confusion when goods moved between them. Converting between systems required tables or specialist knowledge, and a familiar unit name did not always mean a familiar quantity. Shared measures could reduce that work, though adopting them imposed costs of its own. Tools had to be changed, labels rewritten and users trained. Resistance was not necessarily ignorance. A new system could offer broad benefits while asking particular workers to bear immediate expense.
Calibration is the process of comparing an instrument with a suitable reference and establishing how its readings relate to that reference. It does not mean making every instrument perfect. A useful calibration record can describe an error and the uncertainty around it. For example, a workshop may apply a correction when using an instrument rather than replacing it immediately. The important point is that the reading should not be treated as exact merely because it appears as a number. Extra digits on a display can create an appearance of knowledge that the measurement process does not support.
Temperature provides a straightforward example of environmental influence. A material may expand or contract as conditions change, so a physical reference needs specified conditions of use. Handling, storage and comparison procedures become part of the definition in practice. Modern systems aim for references that can be reproduced in different laboratories, but reproducibility still requires procedures and trained judgement. It is misleading to contrast an entirely social past with an entirely objective present. Social cooperation makes technical comparison possible in both cases, even when the scientific basis becomes more stable.
Documentation allows the chain of comparison to be checked. A certificate should identify the instrument, the reference, the conditions and the relevant date. Without traceability, a precise-looking result may be difficult to connect to anything beyond the local device. This matters when several organisations contribute to one product. A component made in one workshop must fit another made elsewhere, and differences may not become visible until assembly. Shared measurement practice allows organisations to investigate a mismatch rather than merely argue about whose number looks more convincing.
Finally, standards must be maintained as living arrangements. A reference that nobody can access, or a procedure that ordinary laboratories cannot follow, may fail despite theoretical elegance. Institutions provide training, comparisons and opportunities to question results. The achievement is not the elimination of every uncertainty. It is the creation of a reliable way to describe and reduce uncertainty for a particular purpose. Standard measures make cooperation possible because they organise disagreement: when numbers differ, there is a route back through evidence, conditions and references instead of only a contest of authority.

passages.title: Reading passage 1 · A city learns to deliver differently
passages.text:
A. Every morning, delivery vans entered the narrow streets around Halden Market carrying goods for small independent shops. Many left almost empty after visiting a single customer. Shopkeepers complained about congestion but resisted a proposal to keep vehicles outside the centre: they depended on reliable deliveries and feared another administrative burden. The eventual experiment began with a practical offer rather than a restriction. A warehouse near the ring road would receive consignments from different suppliers, combine them, and complete the final journey with electric cargo cycles. Participation was voluntary during the first six months.

B. The project manager, Rosa Vale, expected the strongest interest to come from shops selling light, expensive products. In fact, a bakery became one of the earliest regular users. Its flour sacks were too heavy for an ordinary bicycle, but the project's three-wheeled cycles had enclosed load compartments and were designed for commercial loads. The bakery valued predictable arrival times more than the environmental message. Its owner could schedule preparation without leaving a worker watching the street. This response changed the project's publicity, which began emphasising reliability alongside reduced traffic rather than assuming that every business shared the same motivation.

C. Not every product was suitable. A florist found that delicate arrangements moved during sharp turns unless special supports were fitted. A furniture shop continued receiving large tables directly by lorry, though smaller fittings travelled through the warehouse. These exceptions were recorded instead of being treated as embarrassing failures. The manager wanted a service that removed appropriate journeys, not a claim that one vehicle could replace every other vehicle. Staff kept dimensions and handling instructions with each booking so that an unsuitable consignment could be redirected before it reached the loading bay and delayed other customers.

D. The warehouse initially asked shops to make orders by midday for next-morning delivery. This suited some businesses but not restaurants that adjusted purchases after the evening service. A later collection from suppliers was introduced on three nights each week. It increased staffing costs, yet also attracted enough regular users to make better use of the morning cycles. The project did not publish a standard saving per delivery, because costs depended on distance, load and how consistently a shop used the service. Monthly statements instead separated the handling charge from the charge for the final journey.

E. Routes were planned with local knowledge as well as software. The shortest line on a map could involve steep cobbles, steps or a market entrance closed during trading hours. Riders marked these problems on a shared map, and the route planner updated permitted approaches. The city also installed secure loading stands near several shops. Without these, a rider might have to leave a loaded cycle while carrying goods around a corner. Reducing that risk mattered for insurance and for the willingness of riders to accept the work, not simply for the speed of individual deliveries.

F. Evaluating the trial proved more difficult than counting cycles leaving the warehouse. Some suppliers had previously combined deliveries to several shops on a single van trip. Replacing one shop's parcel did not necessarily remove that trip. The evaluation therefore asked suppliers about routes, not just the number of consignments transferred. It also counted travel between suppliers and the warehouse. These additional movements reduced the estimated traffic benefit but made the comparison more credible. The researchers warned that figures from the first months reflected volunteers who were particularly willing to cooperate and might not represent later customers.

G. Residents noticed another change that was absent from the original spreadsheet. With fewer vehicles blocking shop fronts at breakfast time, the pavement became easier to use, especially for people pushing prams. However, some residents objected when cycles were parked across pedestrian routes. The council introduced marked stopping areas and required riders to dismount in the busiest pedestrian section. The scheme's environmental intention did not exempt it from ordinary questions about public space. Shopkeepers were asked to report problems as well as praise so that the trial would not be evaluated entirely through its organisers' expectations.

H. When the six months ended, the service continued with fewer subsidies but a narrower delivery area. Serving distant customers had consumed disproportionate time, while regular central routes were becoming viable. The revised boundaries disappointed some businesses, yet avoided promising universal coverage that the service could not sustain. Halden's experience suggests that delivery reform is partly a problem of coordination: suppliers, shops, riders and street managers must change compatible parts of their routines. A different vehicle helps, but it succeeds within an arrangement of schedules, handling practices and realistic limits rather than through technology alone.

passages.title: Reading passage 2 · Who notices the night?
passages.text:
A. Night-time lighting is often discussed in terms of brightness, but brightness alone describes neither the experience of a street nor its effect on the surrounding environment. A lamp may illuminate a doorway while sending light into bedroom windows or beyond a riverbank. Another may leave a pavement unevenly lit despite producing more total light. In a fictional research programme, the town of Calder investigated where its lighting went and how different people used it. The starting point was not a commitment to darkness. It was recognition that good lighting requires a purpose and a location.

B. Lighting engineer Arun Mehta began by mapping lamps and measuring illumination on the pavement. His map showed large differences between adjacent streets that had been upgraded in different decades. Replacing every old lamp immediately would have exhausted the budget without establishing which changes mattered. Mehta proposed a staged trial in which matched streets received new fittings at different times. Measurements continued on streets awaiting replacement. This arrangement helped separate the effects of the trial from changes affecting the whole town, such as seasonal shifts in commuting and the amount of natural light during evening journeys.

C. Ecologist Beth Rowan examined a footbridge crossing a small stream. Lamps on its railings directed light onto the water as well as the walking surface. She recommended shields that limited the sideways beam. Her team recorded insect activity before and after installation, while also recording wind and temperature. An increase near one lamp could represent attraction to the light rather than growth in the local insect population. Rowan therefore resisted the simple claim that seeing more insects always indicated a healthier site. The pattern of movement mattered, including whether activity was being concentrated away from neighbouring dark areas.

D. For social researcher Cora Blake, a technically uniform pavement was not automatically a comfortable route. She accompanied volunteers on evening walks and asked where they hesitated. Several pointed to the transition from a very bright shopping entrance to a much dimmer side street. Their concern involved sudden contrast rather than the side street's measured brightness alone. Blake also interviewed people who avoided evening walking entirely. Surveying only pedestrians already on the route would have omitted them and exaggerated satisfaction. Her sample was designed to include absence as a form of relevant behaviour, not merely as missing data.

E. Business representative Dan Wu initially feared that reduced lighting would discourage late customers. He agreed to a trial after the council separated decorative lighting from the lights used for entrances and steps. Shop signs could switch off after closing while essential access lighting remained. Wu asked businesses to log actual closing times, since a fixed schedule based on official hours would not cover seasonal events. Some shops closed early on quiet evenings; others held occasional late workshops. A flexible arrangement required more communication than a single town-wide switch, but avoided treating every commercial frontage as if it had identical needs.

F. The trial's energy figures were easier to calculate than its social outcomes. Meter readings showed the electricity used by each circuit, but a fall in reported complaints did not prove that everyone preferred the new lighting. Residents might not know where to report concerns or might assume the decision was final. Blake distributed paper feedback cards as well as an online form and returned to several households that had not replied. These efforts did not create a perfectly representative sample. They did reveal problems that would have disappeared from an evaluation relying exclusively on the most convenient reporting channel.

G. There were disagreements about which results should determine the next investment. Mehta favoured repairing the least efficient circuits, while Rowan wanted attention to a sensitive riverside section that used relatively little electricity. Both positions could be supported by evidence because they pursued different objectives. The council published the trade-off rather than combining every measure into an unexplained score. Its final programme reserved part of the budget for ecological locations and part for general replacement. No claim was made that the chosen division was the only scientific answer; it was a public decision informed by several kinds of expertise.

H. Calder's imagined programme demonstrates why the phrase better lighting cannot be reduced to either more light or less light. A fitting can use less energy and still direct light badly. A well-lit route can still be difficult to enter, and an apparently popular policy can overlook people least likely to comment. The value of the trial lay in making these distinctions observable. It provided a method for revising decisions, not a final design suitable for every street. The town treated lighting as an ongoing service to different users rather than as a product whose quality ended with installation.

passages.title: Reading passage 3 · When a copy is an achievement
passages.text:
A. Originality has an attractive place in accounts of creativity. We celebrate the first version of an idea and often treat later copies as evidence of limited imagination. Yet much skilled activity depends on reproducing something well enough to discover what its description leaves unsaid. A musician learns another player's phrase; a craftsperson reconstructs an old joint; a researcher repeats a procedure. These activities are not equivalent in every respect, but they expose a weakness in the assumption that copying and understanding are opposites. Reproduction can be a demanding way of asking how an achievement became possible.

B. There are, of course, copies whose purpose is deception. An imitation sold as an original painting misrepresents its history, whatever the technical skill involved. Condemning that deception does not establish that all imitation lacks educational value. The relevant question is what claim is made for the copy and what work it enables. A clearly labelled reconstruction invites comparison. A counterfeit prevents it by concealing the distinction on which a fair judgement depends. The difference concerns honesty about provenance as well as visual resemblance, and a discussion that ignores provenance confuses two quite separate kinds of value.

C. In a fictional design class, students are asked to rebuild a simple folding stool from photographs and measurements. Many initially think the task will require little interpretation because the object is so familiar. Difficulties appear when they decide how much clearance the moving parts need and how to assemble joints without trapping the frame. These matters are not obvious in a completed photograph. When students later design their own stools, they can explain why a particular attractive shape will not fold safely. Their copied object has become evidence of decisions, not merely a substitute for the photographed original.

D. This does not imply that accurate reproduction automatically creates transferable expertise. A student can follow a memorised sequence while misunderstanding its purpose. Teachers therefore need to vary the conditions: a different material, an altered scale or a constraint on available tools. If the learner adapts successfully and can justify the adaptation, there is stronger evidence of understanding. The variation is useful precisely because it interrupts effortless repetition. Copying becomes educational when it makes features available for inspection and revision, rather than when it rewards the preservation of an unexamined routine.

E. The same distinction helps explain why a detailed written recipe may fail to reproduce a skilled performance. Experts often omit actions that have become automatic: testing a surface with a fingertip, listening for a change in a tool, or waiting until a material feels right. A novice needs these cues named or demonstrated. Observing a performance and attempting a copy can make such omissions visible to both learner and expert. The expert may then improve the instructions. Knowledge is not simply transferred from a complete document into an empty learner; the act of teaching can reveal that the document was incomplete.

F. Digital tools introduce a different situation. A file can be duplicated with great accuracy without the person pressing the button learning anything about its construction. This is not a criticism of duplication, which is often exactly what the task requires. It is a reminder that similarity in the result does not prove similarity in the process. Rebuilding a model and downloading it can produce indistinguishable outputs while providing very different learning opportunities. Assessments that inspect only the final object therefore need caution if their stated purpose is to evaluate the maker's reasoning, not merely the object's usefulness.

G. Nor should reconstruction erase the social setting of an earlier work. Reproducing a historic tool with modern machinery can demonstrate its geometry while revealing little about the time, labour or organisation once required to make it. A responsible account states which conditions were replicated and which were changed. Such limits do not render the copy worthless. They identify the questions it can answer. An experiment need not recreate an entire past world to be informative, but it must not use success under one set of conditions as proof that the same success occurred under another.

H. The strongest defence of copying is therefore neither that everything is imitation nor that originality is a myth. It is that different activities deserve evaluation against their actual purposes. A copy may preserve access, reveal a hidden technique, test a description or prepare someone to innovate. It may also deceive or merely repeat. We should ask which of these things it does before deciding that its secondary status settles its worth. Creativity includes the ability to depart from a model, but that departure often becomes meaningful only after someone has understood what the model demands.

scripts:
Part 1 · Arranging a bicycle repair visit

Mechanic: Hello, Mobile Cycle Repairs. I’m Sam. What can I do for you?
Customer: My bicycle needs attention, and I wondered whether you could come to my workplace. I can ride it slowly, but I don’t want to use it for my normal journey until it’s been checked. Your website says you cover the northern part of town.
Mechanic: We do. Could I take your surname first, please? Then we’ll check the address and what kind of work may be involved.
Customer: Lennox, L-E-N-N-O-X. The bicycle is quite old, though it was serviced last spring. The brakes feel all right, but the chain slips when I’m pushing hard uphill. A friend suggested changing it myself, but I’d prefer a proper inspection.
Mechanic: That’s sensible. A slipping chain can have more than one cause. We won’t replace anything just on the basis of a telephone description. What kind of bicycle is it: a road model, a mountain bike or something else?
Customer: It’s a folding bike. I take it on the train sometimes, which is why I don’t want to replace it with a larger one. There’s nothing electrical on it.
Mechanic: Fine. For appointments, I could offer Monday afternoon or Wednesday morning. Tuesday is fully booked, and we don’t have an evening round this week.
Customer: Wednesday would be best. I have meetings on Monday. Is nine o’clock possible?
Mechanic: The first slot has gone, but we can be there at ten fifteen. Allow up to an hour for the inspection and ordinary adjustments, though we may need to order a part for a later visit.
Customer: Let’s say 10:15, then.
---
Customer: What is the basic charge?
Mechanic: The inspection and call-out together are thirty-five pounds. That doesn’t include parts, which we’d quote separately. If you decide not to proceed with a repair after the inspection, the basic charge still applies. We used to offer a shorter twenty-pound check, but that no longer includes a workplace visit.
Customer: The office address is on Willow Road. There’s a reception area at the front, but our bicycles are behind the building. Would you want the exact entrance instructions?
Mechanic: Yes, please. We carry tools, so avoiding unnecessary steps helps. Also, tell reception we’re expected; otherwise we can lose half the appointment trying to find the person who booked us.
Customer: Come through the courtyard from the side lane. The gate is usually open during office hours. I’ll put your name on the visitor list and meet you there rather than make you carry equipment through reception.
Mechanic: Good. Is there somewhere dry to work if it rains? We don’t need a full workshop, but a covered area is useful when tools are spread out.
Customer: There’s a shelter beside the staff entrance. It isn’t locked, and there should be room if I move two spare racks. I could ask someone to reserve that space for the morning.
Mechanic: That sounds ideal. Please leave any accessories with us that relate to the fault. And have you still got the key for the folding mechanism’s security lock?
Customer: Yes. I’ll bring the key. I normally leave it at home, so I’m glad you mentioned it. Do you need a receipt from the previous service?
Mechanic: Not essential. You can show us any notes you have, but we’ll inspect the current condition. How would you like to pay?
Customer: By card, if possible. Our accounts team only reimburses expenses with a receipt, so please make sure I get one showing the bicycle work separately from any extra items.
Mechanic: We can do that. We’ll send the confirmation today. If your meeting schedule changes, cancellation is free until noon on the previous working day. After that, we charge for the call-out because we may not be able to fill the slot. Please call rather than relying on an email sent late at night.

Part 2 · Information for volunteers at a food festival

Coordinator: Thanks for volunteering at the town food festival. Some of you helped last year, but the layout and duties have changed, so please listen even if you know the site. We have more small producers this year, and we’ve tried to make unloading less disruptive. The first thing to explain is why the festival is opening an hour later than advertised in the early leaflet. The main road is being resurfaced overnight, and the work crew needs access until eight. Stallholders then need time to set up safely. It isn’t because we expect fewer visitors in the morning.
Visitors are encouraged to come by bus. The usual car park is available, but half of it is reserved for accessible parking and producer vehicles. We aren’t closing it entirely. The temporary shuttle from the station is the most useful addition, since several regular routes don’t operate frequently on Sunday. Please direct people to that service rather than promising that a space will be free when they arrive by car.
If someone asks about ingredients, take them to the stallholder. Volunteers must not make guesses, even if a dish looks familiar. A recipe can change or contain an ingredient you cannot see. Each producer has been asked to provide written information, but the producer remains the right person to confirm it. Our role is to help people reach the information, not to improvise assurance that could be wrong.
The reusable cup scheme is different too. People pay a small deposit and receive it back when they return the cup. We no longer give a voucher for a future event. Several visitors lost those vouchers last year, and others never attended another festival. There are return points at both exits, so no one needs to walk back through a crowded area just to recover the deposit.
Lost children should be brought to the staffed family point near the entrance. Don’t announce a child’s full name over the public address system. Staff there will follow the safeguarding procedure. If an adult approaches you searching for a child, send the adult to the same point rather than taking them on an improvised tour of the stalls.
---
Now I’ll describe the duties for five volunteer teams. The welcome team needs no equipment beyond an identifying jacket. Your key instruction is to remain in pairs. One person can speak to a visitor while the other watches for anyone needing help nearby. You can change partners after your break, but please don’t leave a post unstaffed while both of you fetch a drink.
The tasting team works near the demonstration kitchen. Before starting, you’ll attend a short hygiene briefing with the food coordinator. Previous experience doesn’t exempt you, because the procedure is specific to this event. You won’t be expected to cook, but you will handle small serving trays and need to know which areas must stay separate.
The survey team should collect responses only after visitors have finished at least part of their visit. Please wait until after lunch to begin. Morning arrivals cannot reasonably comment on the whole experience, and asking them at the gate slows entry. The survey isn’t a competition; people are free to decline without being asked twice.
The recycling team will move between several collection points. Wear the protective gloves supplied in your kit. Even clearly labelled bins sometimes contain broken items in the wrong place. You are not required to sort a hazardous object by hand; call the supervisor if you are unsure how to deal with something.
Finally, the photography team must ask permission before taking an identifiable close-up of a visitor. General crowd images are covered by our displayed notice, but a close portrait is different. If someone declines, respect that immediately. We want a record of an enjoyable public day, not a collection of images obtained by making people uncomfortable. Your supervisor can show you examples of what counts as an identifiable close-up.

Part 3 · Designing a visitor-label experiment

Tutor: Tell me how the museum project is developing.
Clara: We want to compare two labels beside the same exhibit. One gives a straightforward description, while the other starts with a question. We’d like to know whether visitors look at the object for longer with the question version.
Rafi: We originally planned to ask which label visitors preferred. But preference wouldn’t necessarily tell us whether they spent more time observing the object itself.
Tutor: Good distinction. How will you avoid changing several things at once?
Clara: We’ll keep the factual information and length similar. The difference should be the opening question, not an extra paragraph of information or a larger typeface.
Rafi: And we won’t put the two versions side by side. People would compare labels rather than use one naturally. We’ll alternate versions across observation periods and record which is displayed.
Tutor: What counts as looking at the object? A visitor could stand there while talking to a friend about lunch.
Clara: We need an operational definition. Our draft says the person’s head is directed towards the exhibit, but that still leaves uncertain cases. We should practise coding the same short video, with permission, and discuss disagreements.
Rafi: The museum has a staged training video made with staff. We can use that rather than recording real visitors just to test our coding sheet.
Tutor: That’s preferable. Who will be in the sample?
Clara: Adults arriving on their own or in groups, but not guided school parties. The guide controls where a school group stops, so their viewing time isn’t comparable with independent visits.
Rafi: We still need to record group size. A family could spend longer because one person wants to stay, even if the label has no effect.
Tutor: And be careful about what your observation can establish. Longer looking may show attention, but it doesn’t prove better understanding. You’d need a different measure for that.
---
Clara: We can add one short question about what visitors think the object was used for. Would that be enough?
Tutor: It might add useful evidence, provided you explain its limited scope. Don’t call it a complete test of learning. Also, it should come after the observed viewing period, or the invitation itself may change how people behave.
Rafi: We need to decide which object to use. We chose a carved wooden box because it isn’t famous and its purpose isn’t obvious from the shape. A well-known object might produce a ceiling effect if everyone already understands it.
Clara: The curator says we can move the box into the side gallery, but moving it would change the context and maybe the number of passers-by. I think we should leave it in its ordinary position.
Tutor: I agree. The display position should remain constant between conditions. You can note changes in nearby activity instead of relocating the object for a tidier-looking experiment.
Rafi: Our draft schedule has observation for ten days. That’s too much for the two of us once seminars start. Would six days across two weeks be reasonable?
Tutor: Yes, as long as your claims match the sample. Six days with careful records is better than ten days with exhausted observers missing entries. Include both busy and quiet periods and specify the schedule in advance.
Clara: We haven’t written the report structure yet. Should we decide on an expected conclusion now?
Tutor: No. Decide what comparisons you will make, not which result you hope to obtain. Keep a log of any departures from the plan. A museum may prefer one label, but your responsibility is to describe what the study can support. An inconclusive result can still show why a more substantial trial is needed.

Part 4 · From textile waste to usable fibre

Lecturer: A discarded garment may look like a straightforward source of material, but recovering useful fibre requires a sequence of decisions. Today we’ll follow a simplified mechanical recycling process for a stream of donated textiles. This is not a description of every industrial method. Different fabrics and desired outputs require different treatments. The point is to understand why collecting a large mass of clothing does not automatically create an equal mass of high-quality new cloth. Each stage changes what is available to the next, and some losses are unavoidable.
The first decision is whether an item should enter recycling at all. Wearable garments may be more useful through reuse. Sorting workers therefore separate items that can still be worn from those intended for material recovery. This stage requires judgement about condition and practical demand, not just age. A nearly new garment with severe damage may be unsuitable for reuse, while an older coat can remain serviceable. Reuse and recycling serve related purposes, but mixing their outputs in one impressive total can hide what actually happens to the collected clothing.
Next, workers examine composition. Labels provide a starting point, though they may be missing or unreliable. A blend contains more than one fibre type, and that combination can make recovery harder. A process designed for a relatively uniform stream may perform poorly on mixed materials. Some facilities use instruments to help identify composition, but readings still need to be interpreted within the process’s limits. Sorting is not merely putting red garments in one pile and blue garments in another; colour and composition answer different production questions.
Colour separation can nevertheless be useful. Keeping similar colours together may reduce the need for later dyeing when the recovered fibre is used in a suitable product. This does not mean every faded shirt can become a new shirt of exactly the same appearance. The final use depends on fibre quality and the specifications of the next manufacturer. A less demanding product may be the realistic destination for some material. Calling that outcome a failure without considering the available alternatives can obscure a useful recovery, while calling it identical to garment-to-garment recycling can also mislead.
Before cutting, workers remove hard components such as buttons and metal fasteners. These can damage machinery or remain as unwanted fragments in the output. Removal takes time, and garment construction affects how easy it is. A designer choosing decorative hardware may therefore influence a future recycling cost without seeing it at the design stage. After preparation, the textile is cut into smaller pieces. The pieces pass through equipment that pulls the fabric apart, releasing fibres rather than preserving the original woven or knitted structure.
Mechanical opening usually shortens fibres. Length matters because very short fibres can be difficult to spin into a strong new yarn. The recovered material may be blended with a proportion of new fibre to meet the intended requirement. The proportion is not a universal recipe: it varies with the input and product. A claim about recycled content should state what is being measured and in which component. A small recycled lining does not make the whole garment entirely recycled, even if the marketing photograph draws attention to the lining.
The output undergoes checks before a manufacturer uses it. Tests may include strength and the presence of unwanted contamination. Sampling needs to represent a batch, not only its cleanest corner. Failed material may enter another suitable route rather than the same spinning process, but that route should be recorded. Mass balances help account for useful output, removed components and losses. Without such records, a collection programme can report what entered the facility while leaving the destination of much of it unexplained.
The broader lesson is that recycling begins before a garment is discarded. Material choice, construction and accurate labelling affect later options. Collection remains necessary, but the quality of the route after collection determines what the activity achieves. A transparent account follows the material through the process, states the intended product and acknowledges limitations. It offers more useful guidance than an unqualified claim that all donated clothing returns to the wardrobe in an endless loop.
