passages.title: Reading passage 1 · Cooling food before the grid arrived
passages.text:
A. Before reliable electricity reached the fictional valley of Orlen, households used several methods to keep food cool. A shaded cellar worked well for some homes, while others stood pots in a stream. Neither arrangement was convenient for the women who sold fresh cheese at the weekly market. Their products travelled for hours in summer, and a cool destination could not undo warming during the journey. A local cooperative therefore investigated containers rather than planning a central cold store. The problem it chose to solve was movement between places, not storage at one fixed location.

B. The first container used a porous outer clay pot, an inner vessel and damp sand between them. As moisture escaped from the outer surface, evaporation removed heat. The design depended on moving air and relatively dry conditions; it was not a miniature refrigerator that could work equally well anywhere. Trials on humid afternoons produced disappointing results. The cooperative kept those records alongside successful tests instead of advertising only the largest temperature fall. A shaded stand improved performance, but enclosing the pot in a sealed cupboard prevented the airflow on which its operation depended.

C. Potter Elin Daro changed the design after watching sellers load their carts. A round pot could roll or tip during transport, and a lid that was easy to lift at home was difficult to secure on a rough track. She added a broad base and a fastening strap. These changes did not improve the cooling mechanism directly, but they reduced spills and breakage. The cooperative discovered that a technically effective object could still be rejected if handling it added work. Users judged the whole trip, including loading and cleaning, rather than one laboratory measurement of temperature.

D. Water supply created another constraint. The sand had to remain damp, but sellers did not want dirty water near food. The revised inner vessel could be removed and washed separately, while a small reservoir fed moisture to the sand. A mark on the reservoir indicated the minimum level before a journey. Sellers were trained to inspect the outer surface for cracks and to replace a damaged vessel. These routines were simple but necessary. Calling the device passive did not mean that it required no attention; it meant that cooling did not depend on a powered compressor.

E. To compare containers fairly, the cooperative placed equal quantities of cheese in them at the same initial temperature. Some travelled in carts, while others stayed on the shaded market stand. A thermometer was read at fixed intervals, and the test sheets recorded air temperature and humidity. The organisers did not ask sellers to taste products that had been stored beyond ordinary safety limits. Cooling performance and food safety were treated as related but distinct questions. A container could slow warming without demonstrating that every kind of food would remain safe for an entire day.

F. The most useful improvement emerged from the trading schedule. Previously, sellers waited until all orders were ready before leaving the village together. Small producers sometimes kept finished cheese waiting for their neighbours. The cooperative organised two departure times, reducing that delay. Better scheduling lowered the demand placed on the containers without changing their construction. Some members initially considered this outside the cooling project, but later recognised that temperature exposure included time before loading. The device was one component of a chain whose other components involved decisions about work, transport and market opening hours.

G. When electricity eventually became available, the clay containers did not disappear immediately. A powered store could hold larger quantities overnight, but the last part of the journey still involved unpowered carts and exposed stalls. Some members used both systems; others abandoned the pots because their routes had become shorter. The cooperative stopped describing one technology as the replacement for the other. Its records instead showed which combination suited which journey. A method could remain useful in a limited role even after a newer system expanded the range of things that the community could do.

H. Orlen's fictional experience illustrates a familiar error in histories of technology: judging an invention only by the device that follows it. A clay cooler looks inadequate beside a modern refrigerator if both are imagined in identical conditions. Real users rarely face that abstract comparison. They consider purchase price, repair, water, travel and the consequences of failure. Understanding their choice requires attention to the service they need, not simply the age of the mechanism. Progress may mean gaining another useful option rather than replacing every earlier practice with a single supposedly universal solution.

passages.title: Reading passage 2 · The gap between knowing and remembering
passages.text:
A. A student who can explain a concept immediately after a lesson may still struggle to recall it a week later. The difference is not necessarily evidence that the lesson failed. Immediate performance and durable access to knowledge are different outcomes, influenced by what happens during and after learning. In a fictional series of classroom investigations, psychologist Nia Vale examined how students judged these outcomes. She was particularly interested in why a method that feels smooth can produce strong confidence without producing equally strong later recall. Her research treated confidence as something to explain, not as a direct measure of learning.

B. In the first investigation, students encountered short accounts of unfamiliar inventions. One group reread each account, while another closed the text and attempted to reconstruct its main points. The second group found the exercise harder and rated its expected later performance less favourably. A week later, however, it recalled more of the central relationships. Vale cautioned that this comparison did not mean reading was unnecessary: both groups needed an initial explanation. The question concerned what learners did after first encountering material, not whether an unsupported attempt could replace every form of instruction.

C. Education researcher Tomas Iven questioned how general the result would be. Recalling a short account under quiet conditions differed from solving a demanding problem in a busy classroom. He designed a follow-up in which learners applied a rule to new examples, some superficially unlike those used in teaching. Performance depended partly on whether the practice required students to explain why the rule applied. Mere repetition of a familiar answer was less helpful. Iven argued that the content of a retrieval attempt mattered as much as the fact that the learner had been asked to remember something.

D. Teacher Sara Omari noticed a practical difficulty in her own classes. When practice attempts were publicly graded, hesitant students sometimes avoided attempting an answer at all. She introduced short private exercises with feedback before using any marks. Students could see a correct explanation after they had committed to an attempt. The change was intended to make an error informative rather than socially costly. Omari did not conclude that all assessment should disappear. She distinguished the function of a practice attempt from that of a final judgement, particularly when students were still deciding whether they could risk exposing a misunderstanding.

E. Another investigation concerned spacing. Learners completed the same amount of practice either in one session or across several days. Spreading it created more occasions on which knowledge had to be brought back after becoming less accessible. Yet the team rejected the slogan that longer gaps were always better. If a gap was so long that learners could recover nothing, frustration replaced useful effort. They adjusted intervals to the material and offered cues where needed. The aim was successful reconstruction with some difficulty, not maximum difficulty as an educational virtue in its own right.

F. Analyst Joel Chen examined how the tests themselves might shape the findings. A later task that repeated practice questions exactly could favour a narrow routine. He therefore included questions requiring explanation in different wording and an application task with a changed surface context. Scores fell compared with the identical-question test, but differences between practice conditions did not vanish. Chen regarded both results as necessary: the fall showed limits, while the remaining difference suggested some transfer. Reporting only the more flattering test would make the intervention look broader than the evidence justified.

G. Students' own study decisions changed only slowly. Many still preferred rereading because a familiar page felt reassuring and because generating an answer exposed gaps they would rather not notice. Vale asked them to predict performance on specific items and then compare those predictions with later results. The exercise made mistaken confidence visible without treating confidence itself as a personal flaw. Some students began using short self-tests voluntarily. Others needed more support, especially when they interpreted an unsuccessful attempt as proof of inability rather than information about what to study next.

H. The fictional investigations do not supply a single timetable or universal recipe. Their shared message is that learning activities should be evaluated against the kind of later performance they are intended to support. An activity may be useful for introducing an idea, another for making it retrievable, and another for extending it to a new context. Feeling fluent during one of these activities is not worthless, but it cannot settle every question. Teachers and learners need evidence that extends beyond the pleasant experience of recognising material while it is still in front of them.

passages.title: Reading passage 3 · The case for a repairable future
passages.text:
A. To describe a product as durable is to make a claim about time, but the claim is incomplete until we know what happens when one part fails. An object may contain excellent materials and still become unusable because a small component cannot be replaced. Conversely, a less imposing object may remain useful through many repairs. Discussions of sustainable design often focus on the moment of manufacture or disposal. The period between them deserves equal attention: this is where ordinary decisions about access, information and maintenance determine how long a product actually serves a purpose.

B. Repairability is sometimes reduced to the presence of screws rather than glue. Accessible fasteners do matter, but access to an internal part is only one step. A user must identify the fault, obtain a suitable replacement, perform the work safely and verify that the object functions afterwards. A product that can be opened easily may still be difficult to repair if its parts have no identifying marks. Design for repair is therefore a property of an arrangement of object, documentation, supply and skills. Treating it as a single visible feature produces reassuring labels without necessarily extending useful life.

C. In a fictional procurement trial, a college compared two models of desk lamp. One was cheaper to purchase and had a sealed light unit. The other cost more but came with a replaceable module and a public parts list. The buyers calculated costs over several years rather than comparing only the invoice. Their result depended strongly on assumptions about failure rates and the continued availability of parts. They published those assumptions, allowing readers to see circumstances in which the cheaper lamp would remain cheaper. A calculation is more informative when its uncertainty is visible than when one favourable estimate is presented as inevitable.

D. Manufacturers can reasonably raise safety concerns. Opening some devices exposes hazards, and an incorrect repair can create risks for users who never performed the work. But safety is not served by leaving a failing product in use because a responsible repair is impossible. The appropriate response depends on the task: some repairs can be supported with clear instructions, while others require trained personnel. A blanket appeal to danger avoids this distinction. The question is not whether every owner should attempt every repair, but whether a workable and proportionate route to repair exists.

E. Information also has an economic role. A business may promise to keep spare parts available but provide no clear price or delivery time. If a replacement costs almost as much as a new object, formal availability gives little practical help. Public buyers can ask for price commitments and delivery expectations before purchasing, not only after equipment fails. These requests will not remove every future uncertainty. They can, however, make maintenance part of competition rather than leaving it as a private inconvenience discovered when the initial sale is complete and the buyer has few alternatives.

F. Consumers are often blamed for preferring novelty, yet their choices reflect the options presented to them. A person offered an immediate replacement and an uncertain repair several weeks away may rationally choose the replacement even while valuing conservation. Convenient repair services can alter this calculation. Loan equipment, clear quotations and local collection points reduce the disruption involved. Moral appeals to keep things longer are unlikely to succeed if the surrounding service makes doing so unusually difficult. Responsibility belongs partly to users, but also to those who shape the time and effort a repair requires.

G. There is a limit to the argument. Keeping every old appliance indefinitely is not necessarily sensible if use consumes far more resources than a replacement would. A comparison should include the impact of making the new product, the expected remaining life of the old one and the difference during use. The balance will vary by product and circumstance. This qualification does not defeat repairability. It prevents repair from becoming a slogan detached from outcomes. A repairable product preserves an option; deciding whether to exercise it still requires judgement about the actual situation rather than automatic loyalty to oldness.

H. A serious repair policy would therefore change more than the construction of objects. It would make long-term support visible at the point of purchase and encourage institutions to retain maintenance knowledge. It would also distinguish repair opportunities from claims that every repair is worthwhile. The goal is neither to freeze technology nor to make consumers responsible for industrial design. It is to ensure that the failure of a small part does not unnecessarily dictate the fate of a whole product. Longevity becomes credible when there is a practical route from breakdown to renewed use.

scripts:
Part 1 · Registering for a bookshop volunteer shift

Organiser: Hello, Page Turners charity bookshop.
Caller: Hello. I saw your notice asking for volunteers. I’ve recently moved to the area and have some free time each week. I’ve worked in a shop before, though not with books. Are you still looking for people?
Organiser: We are, especially for regular shifts. We don’t expect volunteers to know every author. Being willing to ask questions and follow the stock procedure matters more. Could I take your name?
Caller: It’s Nadia Seldon. S-E-L-D-O-N. People sometimes write Sheldon, but there’s no H. I live close enough to walk, so I wouldn’t depend on the bus for an early start.
Organiser: Thank you. Which days could you offer? We have a full team on Saturday at present, but weekday afternoons are more difficult to cover.
Caller: My first thought was Wednesday, but I’ve enrolled on a Wednesday course. I can do Monday every week. I’d rather promise one reliable day than offer several and keep changing them.
Organiser: That would be excellent. The afternoon shift begins at one, but for your first visit please come at twelve thirty. The supervisor can show you the building before customers arrive for the afternoon session.
Caller: All right, 12:30 on Monday. Is it a long shift?
Organiser: Three hours normally. For the induction we’ll keep it to two if you prefer, though it’s useful to see the closing routine on a later visit. You can discuss that with the supervisor when you know your other commitments.
Caller: What kind of work needs doing? I’m happy speaking to customers, but I wouldn’t want to start on the till without training.
Organiser: You won’t. New volunteers usually begin with sorting. Donations come in mixed boxes, and we separate saleable books from items needing specialist advice. You’ll work with an experienced person rather than decide alone what an unfamiliar volume is worth.
Caller: That sounds interesting. Should I bring any documents for the registration?
Organiser: Bring one reference, please, from somebody outside your household. A former work supervisor is fine. We don’t need your school certificates or a formal essay about why you like reading.
---
Caller: Could you explain where to arrive? I know the shop front, but I imagine you don’t want me knocking while it’s closed.
Organiser: Use the rear door on your first day. It’s reached from the small lane beside the café. The front shutters will still be down at twelve thirty, and the bell there isn’t easy to hear from the stockroom.
Caller: I’ll find it. What should I wear? The notice mentioned comfortable shoes.
Organiser: Yes, and ordinary clothes you don’t mind getting dusty. We’ll provide a badge once you’ve registered. Please wear it on the shop floor so customers can tell who is working. There’s no uniform purchase.
Caller: Are volunteers expected to move heavy boxes? I can carry a few books but should avoid lifting something large from the floor.
Organiser: We have a trolley, and heavy boxes should be split into smaller loads. Tell the supervisor about any task you shouldn’t do. Nobody is expected to prove enthusiasm by taking a risk, and there’s plenty of work that doesn’t involve lifting.
Caller: Good. I assume personal belongings stay somewhere away from donations?
Organiser: There are lockers in the office. Please don’t leave a bag on the sorting table, because it could be mistaken for something brought in by a donor. Bring a small padlock if you’d like to lock your locker.
Caller: I have one at home. What if I can’t make a shift after I’ve joined?
Organiser: Call the supervisor as early as possible. Text is fine if the shop is closed, but please don’t just put a message in the social-media group. It can get buried under photographs and general conversation. A direct message lets us arrange cover.
Caller: Understood. I’ll get the reference organised and see you on Monday.
Organiser: I’ll email the induction outline today. Read it before you come if you can, but don’t worry about memorising the stock categories. The first visit is for learning the system, not passing a test.

Part 2 · Tour of the Westfield recreation centre

Guide: Welcome to Westfield. I’ll explain the rooms using the plan on your information sheet, then mention changes to our membership arrangements. You are standing at reception, shown at the bottom of the plan. The corridor runs straight towards the outdoor court at the top. Left and right refer to the direction you’re facing now, not to somebody returning from the court. The central corridor stays clear; equipment should never be left there, even for a minute between classes.
The room immediately to your right is the equipment store. It has double doors, so returning larger items is easier. Members can borrow rackets there, but staff need to record the number before you take them outside. Please don’t help yourself just because another customer has left the door open. Opposite, immediately to your left, is a staff room that is not open to members.
Walk towards the court and you’ll reach two more rooms. The first on the left is the exercise studio. This is where stretching and low-impact classes take place. There are mirrors along one wall, but don’t confuse it with the dance studio at our other building. Across the corridor, the first room on the right beyond the store is the changing area. There are accessible facilities within it, so you don’t need to ask for a separate key at reception.
Continue to the last pair of rooms. On the left, just before the door to the court, is the first-aid room. It is staffed during all organised sessions. On the right is the meeting room, where club organisers can discuss events without standing in reception. That room used to contain vending machines. We’ve moved refreshments into the entrance area to free it for meetings and small training sessions.
---
Outdoor-court bookings are now released seven days ahead. Previously, some members reserved several weeks in advance and then cancelled shortly before playing, leaving little opportunity for others. The shorter window is intended to improve access. It isn’t a response to resurfacing work; that was finished last month and doesn’t affect the current schedule.
Equipment hire is included in the membership price for ordinary sessions. However, lost items must still be paid for. We don’t want members to avoid trying a new sport because they haven’t bought the right racket, but borrowing carries responsibility. If you find a defect before playing, show staff so that it isn’t attributed to you when you return the item.
Our introductory classes have a new attendance rule. You may reserve a place without paying an extra class fee, but if you cannot come, cancel by the previous evening. Two unexplained absences in a month lead to a temporary booking restriction. The aim is to release unused places, not collect penalties from people whose circumstances change unexpectedly.
Children under twelve must be accompanied in the building, except when handed over to a registered children’s class. An adult waiting in the café has not automatically completed that handover. Please speak to the class leader, who keeps a register. If you are collecting for another family, make sure the arrangement has been recorded before the session ends.
Finally, we are looking for feedback on quieter opening periods. We already know that Saturday morning is busy. What we need now is information from people who would use the centre at other times if a particular activity were offered. The short form asks about feasible times as well as preferred activities. A popular suggestion isn’t useful if everyone who chooses it is unavailable when the room can actually be staffed.

Part 3 · Testing a model bridge

Tutor: Your bridge project report is due next week. How did the first test go?
Nora: The model carried more weight than we expected, but it failed suddenly. We thought the main beam would bend first. Instead, a connection near the support pulled apart.
Ethan: We used the right dimensions from the drawing, so at first we blamed the material. Looking again at the video, we saw the connection moving before the beam changed shape.
Tutor: That’s an important observation. A structure is not stronger than every point through which the load must pass. Did you record where each weight was placed?
Nora: Yes, but our first diagram wasn’t precise enough. The weights were spread over a wider area in one test. We need a loading template so that the comparison isn’t affected by where we happen to set them down.
Ethan: We also want to repeat the test on more than one model. Otherwise one badly made connection could be mistaken for the inevitable behaviour of the design.
Tutor: Sensible. Keep construction records so you can discuss differences. Don’t quietly discard a model because it performs less well than you hoped. A poor result may be telling you something about how difficult the design is to build consistently.
Nora: We considered changing the material and the joint together, but then we’d be unable to tell which change mattered.
Ethan: So we’ll first change only the joint, keeping the other dimensions and material the same. If that improves performance, we’ll still need to say how many tests support the claim.
Tutor: Good. What will you count as failure? Total collapse is easy to identify, but a real bridge can become unusable before that.
Nora: We can measure deflection at the centre and set a limit before testing. The report will distinguish exceeding that limit from final collapse.
Tutor: Exactly. A stated criterion makes the comparison meaningful. It also prevents you from redefining success after seeing which version looks best.
---
Ethan: For the next test, we need some equipment. The scale is available in our lab, but the displacement sensor requires booking from the engineering store. We should reserve that today rather than assume it will be there.
Nora: I can arrange the sensor. What about the loading template?
Ethan: That’s the piece we should try out before the main test. The current cardboard version slides when we add weights. If it changes position, the careful markings won’t help us.
Tutor: Make a pilot version and check the practical handling. A procedure can look rigorous on paper and still be impossible to carry out consistently with the hands and space available.
Nora: The safety screen has already been checked by the technician. We have written confirmation, so that item is complete.
Tutor: Keep the confirmation with the risk assessment. Nobody should stand in line with a joint that might release a fragment.
Ethan: Our draft introduction includes a long history of famous bridges. It takes up most of the word allowance without explaining our experiment. We’ll remove that section and use the space for the joint design and testing procedure.
Tutor: A brief context is enough. The reader needs to understand your question, not prove that you have looked at many photographs.
Nora: Finally, the cost comparison. We can’t finish it until we know how much extra material the revised joint uses. We’ll calculate that after constructing the final models.
Ethan: And include labour time separately. A joint that uses very little material but takes much longer to make might not be the better option in every setting.
Tutor: Excellent. Just keep the scope clear. A classroom model can demonstrate a principle and expose construction issues. It cannot certify the safety of a full-size bridge. Your conclusions should be ambitious enough to answer your question and restrained enough to respect that difference.

Part 4 · Designing a household waste audit

Lecturer: A town trying to reduce household waste needs to know more than the weight arriving at a disposal site. It needs an account of what is discarded, where it comes from and which changes could realistically prevent it. Today we’ll follow the design of a fictional waste audit. The first step is to define the boundary. Does the study cover homes only, or also restaurants and offices? If these sources are mixed without a record, a large quantity of food waste might be wrongly attributed to households when businesses produced much of it.
The team then defines the period. A holiday week may differ from an ordinary working week, and one season may not represent the year. Repeating observations can reveal variation, but the budget rarely permits continuous measurement everywhere. Researchers therefore choose sampling dates deliberately and state what they cannot represent. They should avoid selecting only the easiest collection days. A timetable is part of the method, not an administrative detail that can be changed casually once inconvenient conditions appear.
Recruitment matters too. Volunteers who are especially interested in reducing waste may already behave differently from other households. A study based entirely on those volunteers could underestimate ordinary discarding. The fictional team selects addresses from a defined list and makes several attempts to invite each selected household. Participation remains optional, and non-response is recorded. Researchers cannot compel people to share private details. They can, however, describe how the eventual sample differs from the population they hoped to study rather than silently calling it representative.
Before weighing begins, the team establishes categories. Too few categories hide useful distinctions; too many make sorting slow and unreliable. Food that might have been eaten is separated from unavoidable remains within the study’s stated definition. Packaging is classified by material where this can be done consistently. Staff practise on a pilot sample and discuss ambiguous items. A written guide records decisions so that two sorters do not place the same object in different categories simply because each has a different intuition about where it belongs.
Containers have weight of their own. Scales are checked, and the weight of an empty container is recorded so it can be subtracted from the total. Otherwise a heavy collection box could look like a household producing more rubbish. Wet conditions create another complication: absorbed water can alter measured mass. The team records relevant conditions and uses a consistent handling procedure. Apparent numerical precision is not a substitute for knowing what entered the weighing process. A balance showing many decimal places cannot correct a badly defined measurement.
Privacy requires practical arrangements throughout. Bags may contain names, addresses or information about household routines. Staff receive training, identifiable material is not photographed for publicity, and records use codes rather than residents' names. The public report describes groups, not a league table of individual homes. The purpose is to improve a service and identify preventable waste, not embarrass participants into a particular performance. If people fear exposure, they may change what they put out or decline to take part, damaging both trust and the evidence.
Analysis compares like with like where possible. Total weight alone can be misleading when household sizes differ, so the team records the number of residents and considers an appropriate rate. Yet one rate cannot explain every difference: a household may have visitors, work away or use another disposal route. Interviews can add context but also introduce recall errors. The report keeps direct measurements distinct from explanations offered afterwards. This allows readers to see which conclusions rest on the weighing and which remain hypotheses about behaviour.
Finally, an audit should connect its findings to actions that can be checked. If a proposed collection change is introduced, follow-up measurement can ask whether the targeted material actually declines and whether it moves into another stream. A fall in one bin is not automatically a reduction in total waste. The achievement is an evidence-based cycle: define, sample, measure, interpret, act and reassess. Each step makes the next more useful when its assumptions are visible, and each can mislead when a convenient number is treated as the whole story.

passages.title: Reading passage 1 · A harbour makes space for swimming
passages.text:
A. For decades, residents of the fictional port of Esten thought of the inner harbour as a place to work beside rather than enter. Cargo traffic had moved to a larger terminal, but the old quays remained behind fences. When a group proposed an outdoor swimming area, objections concerned more than water quality. Fishing crews still needed access, local businesses feared noise, and some residents doubted that a harbour could feel welcoming. The proposal's supporters began with temporary opening days so that people could experience the site before deciding whether a permanent facility belonged there.

B. Those early days used a floating enclosure close to a disused warehouse. Lifeguards supervised a small number of swimmers, and entry was free. The enclosure kept swimmers separate from boats but did not clean the water. Water testing was therefore essential, and the first opening was cancelled after heavy rainfall. Organisers displayed the cancellation reason at the gate rather than merely posting a notice online. This mattered because some visitors had travelled without checking the website. A disappointing first visit was less damaging to trust when the decision and its evidence were explained clearly.

C. Engineers later traced several drainage routes from streets above the quay. Rain could carry contaminated runoff into the harbour, creating conditions that differed from those measured on dry days. The city improved some drains and introduced a closure protocol based on tests and recent conditions. It did not promise that the swimming area would always be open. Planners considered this uncertainty in the design: a closed pool should not turn the entire waterfront into a dead end. The surrounding deck remained accessible for walking and sitting even when swimming was suspended.

D. Access to the water was another design problem. An ordinary ladder suited confident swimmers but not everyone who wanted to enter. The final enclosure included broad steps and a separate assisted-entry area. Changing cubicles were placed near the entrance, while lockers were visible from the staffed desk. The designers rejected a proposal to locate every service inside the old warehouse because it would force wet swimmers to cross a busy public route. The warehouse instead contained toilets and a classroom used for safety sessions, activities that did not require a direct path from the water.

E. The project also changed who controlled the quay at different times. Fishing crews retained an early-morning unloading period, after which removable barriers opened a wider pedestrian route. A permanent wall would have simplified separation but prevented flexibility. Harbour staff and facility managers met each week during the first summer to resolve problems with delivery times and equipment storage. This routine was less visible than the new deck, yet it made shared use possible. The design depended on agreements that could be adjusted when a fishing boat arrived later than expected or a public event required more space.

F. Counting visitors was straightforward; deciding whom the project served was not. An online survey produced many replies from confident swimmers who had visited repeatedly. Community worker Lena Moss also spoke to older residents at a nearby housing centre and parents at a school. Some liked the waterfront but did not want to swim. Others worried about the cost of lessons rather than admission. Their responses led to a small programme of free introductory sessions. The aim was not to persuade everyone to become a swimmer, but to remove an avoidable barrier for people who wanted to try.

G. By the third summer, the swimming facility had become one attraction among several. A café leased part of the warehouse and helped cover running costs, but its tables occupied only a marked section of the deck. The council wanted to avoid turning a publicly funded waterfront into a place where every seat required a purchase. Free benches remained along the edge, including some outside the busiest view. Maintenance budgets covered replacement of weathered boards and checks of underwater fittings. These recurring expenses were included in public reports alongside attendance, rather than hidden behind the celebration of construction.

H. Esten's fictional harbour was not transformed by a single architectural gesture. Its new use depended on testing, drainage work, access design, operating agreements and attention to people absent from the first survey. Nor did the change erase the port's working identity: fishing activity continued, and swimmers sometimes waited for a delivery to pass. The project suggests that opening a waterfront can mean negotiating a sequence of compatible uses rather than excluding everything that came before. Public access became credible because the city explained its limits and maintained the arrangements that allowed different activities to share a constrained space.

passages.title: Reading passage 2 · Reading the ground without digging
passages.text:
A. An archaeological site does not end at the objects visible on its surface. Buried walls, filled ditches and changes in soil may extend across a much wider area. Excavation can reveal them in detail, but it is slow and changes the deposits it examines. Archaeologists therefore use survey techniques to decide where questions are most promising before opening trenches. In an imagined investigation at North Field, a team compared several ways of reading the ground. None offered an underground photograph. Each measured a physical property from which the team had to infer a possible history.

B. Survey specialist Ada Bell began with aerial images taken after a dry period. Some patches of vegetation had grown differently where buried features altered access to moisture. The marks were useful but inconsistent: a feature visible in one season could disappear in another. Bell compared images from several years and checked whether apparent lines followed modern farm machinery. A striking shape was not automatically ancient. She also recorded blank areas, resisting the temptation to draw a site boundary around only the most attractive marks. Absence in an image might reflect conditions rather than absence in the ground.

C. Geophysicist Ben Ortiz then used an instrument that detected small magnetic variations. In suitable conditions, disturbed soil and some heated materials can differ from surrounding deposits. At North Field, however, recent metal fragments produced strong signals that obscured subtler ones. Ortiz mapped these disturbances rather than simply smoothing them away. The cleaned display was easier to read, but he retained the raw measurements so that later users could see how processing affected interpretation. A visually tidy image can communicate certainty that the underlying observations do not deserve, especially when unexplained noise has been removed.

D. Another team, led by Celine Park, measured electrical resistance along selected lines. Moisture affects how easily current passes through soil, so a buried wall might differ from a filled ditch. Recent rain changed the overall readings, making comparisons between separate days difficult. Park introduced reference measurements in an unchanged strip of ground before each session. These did not solve every problem, but they helped identify variation associated with conditions rather than archaeology. Her results supported one of the magnetic features while leaving another uncertain. The disagreement was treated as a reason for a better question, not a competition to choose one winning instrument.

E. Local historian Dev Rao contributed maps and accounts of land use. A rectangular feature that excited the team as a possible early building appeared at the location of a much later livestock enclosure. The map did not prove the interpretation, because its scale and alignment were imperfect. It nevertheless offered an alternative that had to be considered. Rao also interviewed farmers who remembered changes in drainage. Their recollections were recorded with dates and qualifications rather than treated as either unquestionable truth or mere anecdote. Different evidence carried different uncertainties, and comparison required preserving those distinctions.

F. The team eventually opened two small trenches. One confirmed a stone foundation, while the other exposed a modern drain where a promising linear signal had appeared. This mixed result was more useful than a simple success story. It showed that the survey had located real differences in the ground without always identifying their cause correctly. The trench records were linked to the survey archive, including the unsuccessful interpretation. Future researchers would therefore be able to revisit the decision process instead of seeing only the feature that justified the team's original enthusiasm.

G. There was also a question of where not to dig. A patch containing fragile deposits was left untouched because the immediate research question could be answered elsewhere. Non-invasive survey did not make excavation unnecessary; it helped target an irreversible action. The landowner wanted assurance that the whole field would not be opened, and a public explanation described the planned limits. Protecting archaeological information involved preserving some uncertainty. A feature could remain an informed possibility until a future project had a compelling reason and a suitable method to investigate it more directly.

H. North Field's fictional investigation illustrates the difference between detecting a pattern and explaining it. Instruments extend perception, but their outputs become evidence through decisions about conditions, processing and comparison. A survey image can look authoritative while concealing several plausible interpretations. Good reporting makes that uncertainty usable rather than merely adding a vague warning at the end. The result is a map of questions as well as features: where evidence agrees, where it conflicts, and where a future observer might learn something new without repeating damage that has already been done.

passages.title: Reading passage 3 · Who should explain a decision?
passages.text:
A. When an institution uses a model to rank applications, explanation can appear to be an optional courtesy added after the result. A person receives a decision and perhaps a sentence describing the system's general purpose. Yet decisions allocate opportunities, and an explanation may be necessary for identifying an error or challenging an inappropriate rule. The question is not simply whether the model can produce a plausible account of its operation. It is whether the institution gives the affected person information that serves a practical purpose, together with a route for acting on it.

B. Different audiences require different explanations. An engineer investigating a calculation may need a detailed account of data transformations. An applicant may need to know that an outdated address caused the system to assign the wrong eligibility category. Providing the engineer's report to the applicant can satisfy a formal requirement while failing to help. Technical completeness and practical intelligibility are not identical. An institution should begin by asking what the recipient must be able to understand or do, rather than assuming that more mathematical detail always makes a decision more accountable.

C. Consider a fictional scholarship programme. Its ranking model awards additional weight to applicants from areas with limited educational resources. An applicant who recently moved is assigned to a better-resourced area using an old record. Explaining that neighbourhood data influenced the score is useful, but incomplete. The applicant needs to know which address was used and how to correct it. More importantly, the programme needs a procedure for reviewing the decision after correction. Information without a responsive process may merely describe an injustice accurately while leaving its consequence unchanged.

D. Explanation also has limits when the rule itself is disputed. A perfectly accurate account of a policy does not make the policy fair. People may agree on how a model treated distance from a training centre while disagreeing on whether distance should count at all. This disagreement cannot be resolved by showing that the software performed its calculation correctly. It requires institutional reasons and, where appropriate, public debate. Technical auditing remains valuable, but it answers a narrower question than the legitimacy of the objective that the institution has instructed the system to pursue.

E. Some critics argue that explanations will enable people to manipulate a system. The concern is real when a disclosed threshold allows someone to alter a superficial signal without meeting the policy's purpose. Nevertheless, secrecy can also shield errors and arbitrary rules. Institutions need to distinguish exploitable operational details from information necessary for a meaningful challenge. An applicant should not have to accept a demonstrably false record merely because the ranking method is commercially sensitive. The burden of finding an appropriate form of disclosure belongs primarily to the institution using the system, not to the person affected by it.

F. Nor is an appealing explanation necessarily faithful. A model can generate a simple story that sounds reasonable without identifying what actually determined its output. If staff repeat such stories without checking them, explanation becomes a technique for discouraging questions. A useful account should be tested against the decision process and should state where certainty is limited. In some cases the honest answer is that a particular contribution cannot be isolated reliably. That admission may be less satisfying than a confident narrative, but it gives a reviewer a more accurate basis for deciding whether further investigation is needed.

G. Human review is often offered as a remedy, although the phrase can conceal very different arrangements. A reviewer with no time, authority or additional information may simply confirm the original result. Meaningful review requires the ability to change it and a reasoned record of the judgement. It also requires attention to recurring patterns: correcting one applicant's address should lead the programme to ask whether similar errors affect others. Otherwise an appeal system can become a costly way of repairing individual cases while leaving a predictable source of harm operating unchanged.

H. Accountability therefore belongs to an institution, even when a complex model makes part of its work difficult to describe. A supplier may assist with analysis, but cannot absorb the public body's responsibility to justify the service it provides. Good explanations connect facts, rules and remedies in language suited to the recipient. Their value lies not in making every refusal pleasant or every dispute disappear, but in making mistakes contestable and policy choices visible. A decision becomes more accountable when the person receiving it can do more than admire the sophistication of the machinery behind it.

writing.prompt: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. The diagram shows a proposed industrial process for turning used cork stoppers into floor panels. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
writing.passage:
Accessible diagram transcription:

1. Collect used cork stoppers.
2. Sort: reject non-cork items (leave the process).
3. Wash accepted cork.
4. Dry with warm air.
5. Grind into granules.
6. Mix granules with a supplied binder.
7. Press the mixture into panels using heat and pressure.
8. Inspect panels: suitable panels go to packing and sale; unsuitable panels are ground again and returned to the mixing stage.

The binder enters only at mixing. The diagram supplies no times, temperatures or quantities.
writing.explanation: Give an overview of collection, preparation, manufacture and inspection, including the feedback loop. Distinguish rejected non-cork input leaving the process from failed cork panels returning to grinding/mixing. Mention binder input and heat/pressure without inventing numerical conditions. This is an authored proposed process, not a claim about every cork factory. A qualified human reviewer should assess task achievement or response, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource and grammatical range and accuracy. No automatic band is assigned.

writing.explanation: Evaluate flexible hours, rather than discussing only home working. Explain benefits and costs for workers or organisations and make a clear comparative judgement. Coordination, service coverage and caring responsibilities are relevant examples. A claim that there are advantages and disadvantages without weighing them leaves the main question unanswered. scripts:
Part 1 · Booking a short residential course

Administrator: Oak House adult learning centre. How may I help?
Caller: I’d like information about the weekend course on making radio programmes. I’ve listened to the sample online and it sounds practical, but I need to check accommodation and travel before booking. I’ll be coming from another town.
Administrator: Certainly. The course includes a room on Friday and Saturday nights, though meals have separate arrangements. Could I take your surname in case we need to continue the booking later?
Caller: It’s Varden, V-A-R-D-E-N. I’ve never stayed at the centre. Is the building close to public transport, or would I need to hire a car?
Administrator: You won’t need a car. Come to Brook station, not the larger station at Hillgate. People sometimes choose Hillgate because more trains stop there, but the onward connection is much less convenient. From Brook there’s a local bus that stops at our gate.
Caller: I can get there on Friday evening. What time can I collect the room key? The train I’d prefer arrives at about five.
Administrator: Reception opens for arriving residents at four thirty, so 4:30 is the earliest. Before then the rooms are being checked. If your train is later, someone will be here until eight. Please tell us if you expect to arrive after that rather than assuming the front door will stay open.
Caller: Fine. What is the full course fee? I saw two prices on an old leaflet.
Administrator: The residential weekend is one hundred and sixty-eight pounds. The lower figure, one hundred and twenty, is for people who attend teaching sessions but sleep elsewhere. It isn’t a discount available just because you’re travelling by train. Your booking would be £168 before optional meals.
Caller: And how much do I pay to secure a place?
Administrator: A deposit of forty pounds. The rest is due two weeks before the course. We can hold a provisional place until tomorrow while you check the trains, but it isn’t confirmed until we receive the deposit.
---
Caller: Are the rooms shared? I’m happy working with other people all day, but I’d prefer somewhere quiet in the evening.
Administrator: Most are single rooms. There are a few twins for friends booking together, but we never assign a stranger to share without agreement. You’ll have a single room. Towels are included; bring your own toiletries.
Caller: What about meals? I don’t eat meat, and sometimes a residential course provides only a sandwich if you mention it too late.
Administrator: We can provide vegetarian meals. Please put vegetarian on the booking form rather than only telling the tutor, because the kitchen uses the form to plan. Breakfast is included in the room price. You can buy lunch and dinner here or use places in the village.
Caller: Do participants need to bring recording equipment? I have a laptop, but no special microphone.
Administrator: We’ll provide microphones and recorders. Bring headphones if you have a comfortable pair. We have some spares, but people often prefer their own for editing. Your laptop can be useful, though it’s not a requirement and we can supply a shared computer.
Caller: I may have a large bag because I’m continuing to visit family afterwards. Is there somewhere to leave it on Sunday after checkout?
Administrator: Yes, bags can stay in the office until the last session ends. They shouldn’t be left in the corridor, which is an emergency route. The workshop itself is on the ground floor, so you won’t need to carry the bag upstairs and down again.
Caller: Good. Is there preparation to complete before arriving?
Administrator: Please bring a photograph of a place you know. You’ll use it as a starting point for a short spoken piece. It needn’t be artistic, and it won’t be assessed as a photograph. We’re interested in the story it helps you tell, not the camera you used.
Caller: That sounds manageable. I’ll check the train now and complete the form tonight.
Administrator: I’ll send the travel sheet and provisional booking reference. Check the dates before paying, as there is a second radio course in the following month and the accommodation arrangements differ slightly.

Part 2 · A guide to the town’s open-building weekend

Guide: Welcome to the information session for our open-building weekend. Several places normally closed to the public will offer visits, and the arrangements differ between sites. Please don’t assume that the ticket for one building lets you enter all the others. Most visits are free, but we still need to manage numbers and protect working spaces. I’ll explain five buildings first, then some general advice for planning your day. The leaflet contains addresses, and the updated website has the latest cancellation information.
The old courthouse is popular because people want to see the hearing room and the cells below. Only a limited number can enter each tour, so you must reserve a timed place before the weekend. We won’t maintain a queue for spare places at the door. If you can’t attend, cancel so someone else can use it. Booking several times in the hope of deciding later makes this much harder.
The clock workshop is reached by a steep staircase. There is no lift, and the narrow turn means we cannot install a temporary ramp. The ground-floor display remains available to everyone, but a visit to the workshop itself involves stairs. The leaflet states this clearly because we don’t want someone travelling across town only to discover the restriction on arrival.
At the recording studio, visitors can try making a short sound effect under supervision. Bring nothing special; the materials are supplied. The session is designed around participation rather than standing silently while someone describes equipment. Your recording can be sent to you afterwards if you choose to provide an address, but you don’t have to give one to take part.
The water tower offers the best view, but its opening depends on conditions. Strong wind makes the exposed upper platform unsuitable for visitors. Check the morning update before leaving home. We don’t cancel just because it’s cloudy, but safety takes priority over keeping a promise printed weeks earlier. A closure there doesn’t mean every other building will be closed.
The municipal greenhouse will stay open later than the other sites, until eight in the evening. That may help people who work during the day. Please use the marked paths because staff will still be maintaining plants in some sections. You can see those activities, but the site isn’t being converted into an unrestricted evening park.
---
For travel, we recommend the temporary circular bus. A ticket covers repeated journeys during the day, and the bus stops near all five sites. Walking between two nearby buildings is easy, but the whole circuit is longer than it appears on the small leaflet map. The service is intended to make combinations possible, not to require visitors to see every location in one day.
Please arrive for a reserved tour about ten minutes early. Earlier than that, there may be nowhere suitable to wait. A guide cannot delay the start for late arrivals because the next group needs its own full visit. If you miss a start, contact the booking desk rather than attempting to join through a side entrance.
Photography rules vary. You may photograph public displays where signs permit, but working documents on desks are not part of the exhibition. Ask before taking an identifiable photograph of an employee. Some are doing their ordinary jobs while visits take place, and being visible to the public isn’t agreement to appear in somebody’s online album.
Children are welcome on the family routes shown in the leaflet. Other tours include lengthy explanations or restricted spaces, so please read the age guidance. It isn’t a judgement about whether a particular child is well behaved. It’s information about what the organiser can provide safely and comfortably within that building.
At the end of a visit, you may be invited to suggest questions for next year’s programme. We particularly want to know what you’d like to understand about the work done inside these buildings. Requests simply to open more places are welcome, but a specific question helps us plan a useful visit rather than merely unlock another door. Staff have volunteered their time, and good questions make the exchange rewarding for them too.

Part 3 · Preparing a student radio feature

Tutor: You’ve brought a draft plan for your radio feature. What’s the focus now?
Lena: We started with a general history of the night bus. It sounded too much like a list of dates, so we’re focusing on the people who use the last service and what the journey means in their routines.
Omar: We’d like to include different voices without pretending that three interviews represent everyone who travels at night.
Tutor: Good. What sound will help listeners understand the setting?
Lena: We recorded the bus arriving, but the engine overwhelms most of the conversation at the stop. We shouldn’t just turn up the voices because that also makes the background louder.
Omar: We could use a short arrival sound separately, then conduct the interviews a little way from the road. The sound can establish the scene without sitting under every spoken sentence.
Tutor: That would improve clarity. Remember that an atmospheric recording is useful only if it serves the story. You don’t need continuous noise to prove you were there.
Lena: We interviewed one passenger already. He gave a lovely account, but asked not to be identifiable. Could we keep the voice and omit the name?
Tutor: A distinctive voice or workplace detail may still identify him. Discuss the intended use with him and offer an alternative, such as reading an agreed extract with another speaker. Don’t assume that removing a name solves every privacy issue.
Omar: The transport office offered an official spokesperson. We should include that view, but perhaps not let it be the only explanation of why the timetable changed.
Tutor: Exactly. Ask which records support the explanation, and compare it with other evidence. Official status is relevant to the speaker’s role, not a guarantee that every interpretation is complete.
Lena: Our biggest editing problem is that all the interviews are interesting. We have enough for twenty minutes but the assignment allows eight.
Omar: We need to return to the central question and select material that advances it, even if a favourite anecdote has to go.
Tutor: That’s the discipline. Cutting should be guided by purpose, not by whether a sentence is easy to remove without changing your preferred argument.
---
Lena: We’ve divided the remaining work into five items. The opening sequence is drafted, but we want to play it to someone who hasn’t heard the story. If they can’t identify the setting and question, we should revise it.
Omar: The permission for the passenger extract is still unresolved. We’ll contact him again before using anything, not treat the earlier interview as blanket consent.
Tutor: Good. Put that ahead of polishing transitions. A beautifully edited extract you can’t use isn’t progress towards a finished feature.
Lena: The transport timetable is checked. We compared the current version with the archived one and confirmed the change date with the office, so that part is complete.
Omar: Our long music introduction is another matter. It takes almost a minute, which is too much in an eight-minute programme. We’ll remove it and retain only a brief transition where it helps listeners follow the change of scene.
Tutor: Ensure you have rights to whatever music remains. There is no need for a grand opening merely because professional programmes sometimes use one.
Lena: The final title is undecided. We have a working title, but we’ll choose the public one after the edit, when we know what the piece actually emphasises.
Omar: Otherwise we might force the material to fulfil a clever title we invented before listening properly. We’ll keep a few alternatives and ask what each one promises the audience.
Tutor: Sensible. When you deliver, include a short production note describing major editorial choices. Listeners won’t hear every decision, but the note should explain why you selected voices, separated sound from speech and omitted material. It makes the learning visible without turning the feature itself into a lecture about editing.

Part 4 · Place names as historical evidence

Lecturer: A place name can remain familiar long after the feature it once described has disappeared. A street called Mill Lane may contain no mill, and a district named after a field may now be covered with houses. Today we’ll consider how names can contribute to historical enquiry and why they should not be treated as complete records by themselves. Our examples come from an invented district, so the purpose is to explain a method rather than make claims about a particular real community’s language or origins.
The first step is to collect forms of the name from different periods. Modern spelling may conceal earlier variations, and a single old map may contain an error. Researchers compare maps with deeds, directories and other dated documents. The sequence does not always show a neat progression from one form to another. Two spellings may coexist for many years. A record should preserve that variation instead of silently converting every historical form into the version printed on today’s sign, because the difference itself may be relevant evidence.
Pronunciation adds another source. Residents may say a name in a way that differs from what an outsider expects from its spelling. Interviews can preserve these spoken forms, though no individual speaker automatically represents an entire district. Age, neighbourhood and family history may all matter. With permission, researchers record speech and note the context of the interview. A recording without information about who was speaking and when can become difficult to interpret later, even when the sound quality is excellent.
Meaning is particularly tempting. A familiar modern word may appear inside a name, inviting an easy story about its origin. Yet the resemblance could be accidental, or the form could have changed from a different earlier word. Researchers need historical and linguistic evidence before accepting the attractive explanation. Local stories remain valuable as accounts of how residents understand a place, but that is not identical to demonstrating how the name first arose. The two questions can be studied together without pretending they have the same answer.
Maps also reveal spatial uncertainty. A name may move from a small feature to a larger area, or survive after a road is redirected. The modern boundary of a neighbourhood should not automatically be projected backwards onto every old reference. Researchers record what geographical extent a document appears to mean. Sometimes a description of adjoining properties is more useful than a bold label at the centre of a map. Names belong to practices of locating and describing places, not merely to fixed points waiting unchanged through time.
Official renaming creates another layer. A council decision may introduce a new name on signs while residents continue using the old one. Administrative records establish the formal change date, but everyday adoption can be gradual and uneven. Delivery workers, schools and local newspapers may use different forms. Studying that transition requires several kinds of evidence. A decree tells us what was authorised, not exactly what everyone said the following morning. Treating official documents as a complete account of usage would miss a large part of the social history.
The project must also consider consent and sensitivity. Some names carry associations that residents find painful, while others are closely connected with a minority community’s identity. Publishing an origin story can affect present debates, even when the researcher thinks of the work as purely historical. This is not a reason to suppress evidence, but it is a reason to explain uncertainty and consult people who may be affected. A neat public label should not turn a disputed interpretation into an apparently settled fact just because a display has limited space.
Finally, a useful catalogue links each claim to its source. It separates an attested form from a proposed meaning and records alternatives where the evidence remains inconclusive. The aim is not to make every name mysterious. Some have clear and well-supported histories. It is to prevent the ease of repeating a story from being mistaken for the strength of its evidence. Names can connect everyday journeys to a deeper history when researchers preserve the route by which they reached their conclusions, including the points where that route still divides.
