passages.title: Reading passage 1 · A library beyond its walls
passages.text:
A. The fictional district of Wendon contained a modern central library and several villages whose residents rarely visited it. Bus services were infrequent, and opening hours overlapped with many people's working day. The district's first response was to advertise its online collection more widely. That helped some readers but assumed access to reliable connections and suitable devices. Librarian Noor Hale proposed a different experiment: small staffed collection points in places people already used. The aim was not to reproduce a full library in every village, but to reduce the effort needed to obtain particular services.

B. A room beside a food shop became the first collection point. Residents could request books from the central catalogue and collect them during two weekly sessions. Hale rejected the suggestion that requests should be made exclusively online. A telephone line and paper slips allowed people to use the service without learning a new interface. Staff entered those requests into the same system, so stock records remained consistent. This extra work was counted in the project budget rather than treated as free labour that would somehow be absorbed by existing staff alongside all their other duties.

C. Choosing a venue involved compromises. A village hall had more space, but stood on the outskirts and opened mainly for planned events. The food shop offered less room but attracted regular visits. The library paid a modest rent for the adjoining room and installed a lockable cabinet for requested items. Books were not left on open shelves overnight. A small selection was available for browsing during staffed sessions, yet most of the stock remained at the central building. This preserved the benefit of a shared collection rather than dividing it into tiny permanent holdings.

D. Transport initially followed a fixed route on one morning each week. A missed request could therefore produce a long wait. The team added a late request deadline for urgent educational materials and arranged space in a council vehicle already travelling between offices. This did not create an on-demand courier service, but reduced some avoidable delays without requiring a dedicated journey. The timetable was printed beside request forms. Residents could see when an item was likely to arrive instead of receiving an optimistic promise that staff could not reliably keep.

E. The collection point also attracted questions unrelated to borrowing. People asked for help understanding forms, finding local history photographs and using audio books on a phone. Hale trained staff to recognise when they could help and when a specialist referral was needed. The library did not collect copies of private financial documents or complete applications on residents' behalf. A quiet screen allowed conversations to be less audible to other visitors. These boundaries protected both users and staff while acknowledging that access to information often begins with a question more complicated than a book title.

F. After six months, the district compared borrowing records with a short household survey. Borrowing had increased, but the survey showed that some residents still did not understand which services were available. Others knew about the point but could not attend either weekly session. One opening was moved to an evening after consultation with shop staff. The evaluation also distinguished new users from existing library members who had simply switched collection location. Both groups benefited, but confusing them would exaggerate how many previously excluded people the experiment had reached.

G. Expansion brought a new concern: volunteers offered to run additional points without paid staff. Their enthusiasm was welcome, yet Hale argued that a reliable public service could not depend entirely on whoever happened to be free. Volunteers helped with publicity and reading events, while trained employees retained responsibility for records, privacy and referrals. The district expanded to three more venues, with a published rota and cover for absence. Growth was slower than a volunteer-only model might have allowed, but opening times became a commitment residents could plan around rather than an informal possibility.

H. Wendon's experiment did not make the central library redundant. Its collection, professional expertise and specialist spaces supported the smaller points. Nor could a collection cabinet provide everything that a welcoming building offered. The district described the service as a network with different functions rather than a contest between physical and digital access. Its achievement lay in connecting shared resources to ordinary journeys and offering several ways to ask for help. The lesson was not that libraries require fewer people, but that their people and materials can be organised around the obstacles that prevent use.

passages.title: Reading passage 2 · Watching change one picture at a time
passages.text:
A. Pictures contributed by the public can form a record of environmental change, but an attractive collection of images is not automatically a comparable dataset. A photograph of a tree may show its leaves clearly while revealing little about the date, location or conditions of observation. In a fictional project called Seasonal Streets, researchers invited residents to photograph selected trees throughout the year. The project sought to understand local differences in seasonal events, not to identify the single earliest leaf in the country. Its success depended on ordinary observations being repeated in sufficiently consistent ways.

B. Project scientist Lina Moss designed a simple protocol. Participants chose a marked viewing position and included the same branch in each picture. They also recorded the date and whether buds, open leaves or fallen leaves were visible. Moss knew that these categories compressed a continuous process into discrete labels. She supplied examples of borderline stages and allowed an uncertain category. Requiring a definite answer for every image would create apparent precision by hiding genuine disagreement. The project preferred a visible gap in certainty to a confident classification that the photograph could not support.

C. Photographer Evan Cole worried that participants would move to obtain a more appealing composition. He demonstrated why a less beautiful but consistent viewpoint was often more useful. If one week showed a sunny outer branch and the next showed the shaded centre of the tree, an apparent change could reflect framing rather than development. Cole made a short guide using deliberately ordinary photographs. The purpose was not to train residents as professional photographers. It was to show which visual decisions affected the comparison and which, such as including an untidy fence in the background, usually did not matter.

D. Analyst Priya Nair examined missing observations. Trees near busy routes attracted more photographs, while those at the end of quiet streets were often neglected. A period of bad weather produced fewer submissions even though seasonal change continued. Nair warned against interpreting the average of submitted pictures as if the same places had been observed on every date. She tracked each tree separately and reported the number of observations behind each summary. Participants could then see why a smooth town-wide curve might conceal irregular evidence and why more photographs did not necessarily mean a more representative sample.

E. Community organiser Hugo Reyes concentrated on who could participate. A phone-based submission tool was convenient, but some residents preferred a camera and a paper record. The project offered monthly drop-in sessions where staff uploaded those images with the contributor. Reyes also arranged pairs so that a participant away from home could ask another person to photograph the same branch. These arrangements made continuity a shared responsibility. They did not eliminate all barriers, but they avoided treating ownership of a recent smartphone and constant personal availability as necessary qualifications for noticing a local tree.

F. The first year's results showed earlier leaf development on several sheltered streets. The team resisted attributing the entire difference to temperature because tree species, age and management also varied. A second phase added paired observations of the same species in contrasting locations. It also recorded pruning, which could remove the photographed branch or change the exposure of the remaining leaves. These additions emerged from uncertainty in the first phase rather than from an attempt to make the initial findings sound more decisive. An exploratory project can be useful by revealing what a later comparison needs to control.

G. Participants reported benefits that were not part of the scientific measurement. Some began noticing insects or discussing the street's history with neighbours. The team welcomed these outcomes but kept them separate from claims about the quality of the seasonal data. A socially valuable activity can still generate uneven evidence, and a rigorous measurement can still be unwelcoming to many residents. Evaluating both purposes required more than a single participation total. The organisers asked what people learned, which observations were usable and whose experience remained absent, without expecting one measure to answer all three questions.

H. Seasonal Streets illustrates a productive relationship between public participation and technical care. Standardisation did not require eliminating every personal contribution; it identified the details that had to remain stable for a particular question. Flexibility elsewhere made participation possible. The photographs became evidence through context, repetition and honest reporting of omissions. Their greatest strength was not that many people could collect pictures cheaply. It was that repeated local attention could connect an abstract question about change with a visible object in everyday life, while leaving enough information for someone else to assess the resulting claim.

passages.title: Reading passage 3 · Is convenience always a gain?
passages.text:
A. Convenience is usually presented as an obvious benefit: a task takes less time, demands fewer steps or can be completed from home. These improvements can matter greatly, particularly to someone with limited mobility or inflexible working hours. Yet a service can become more convenient for its typical user while becoming harder for others to use. A change may also move effort from a paid worker to the customer without making that effort disappear. To evaluate convenience seriously, we need to ask whose effort is counted, when it occurs and which alternatives remain available.

B. Consider a fictional sports centre that replaces its staffed booking desk with an application. Regular players can reserve a court in seconds, even when the building is closed. For them, the change is a clear improvement. A visitor with an older phone, an unfamiliar payment card or limited reading ability may face several failed attempts before receiving help. Counting the average booking time among successful app users excludes these attempts by definition. The resulting figure can be accurate as a description of one group and misleading as a description of the service as a whole.

C. This is not a reason to preserve every inconvenient process. Staffed desks also impose costs: journeys, queues and restricted hours. The stronger conclusion is that comparisons need a complete account of the work involved. A user who spends twenty minutes setting up an account may recover that time over many later bookings, while an occasional visitor may never do so. Initial effort and repeated effort should therefore be distinguished. The same design can be highly convenient for frequent use and poorly suited to a task someone needs only once a year.

D. Automation can also remove small conversations that previously performed an unrecognised function. A receptionist might notice that a new player has booked an unsuitable court or explain a cancellation rule before payment. An application can provide equivalent guidance, but only if the designers know the conversation mattered. Replacing a desk with a form while copying only its visible transaction may omit the informal checking around it. What looked like wasted time may have prevented later mistakes. The task is to identify useful interactions, not to assume that every human exchange is either essential or inefficient.

E. There is a further issue of control. A convenient subscription renewal can prevent an interruption, but a difficult cancellation can turn convenience into one-sided dependence. Friction is the effort a process imposes. Removing it from joining while retaining it in leaving serves the provider more clearly than the customer. Some friction is legitimate, such as confirming a decision with serious consequences. Its justification should depend on the decision's risk rather than on whether the provider benefits from delay. A service that makes actions easy only when profitable offers a selective kind of convenience.

F. Support routes matter especially when a standard process fails. A beautifully designed form cannot anticipate every circumstance, and repeating the same instructions is not useful when the instructions assume something false about the user. An effective exception route allows a person to describe the problem to someone with authority to resolve it. This route may be used rarely and still be essential. Its value should not be judged solely by the proportion of routine transactions it handles, just as an emergency exit is not evaluated by how often people choose it for ordinary entry.

G. Organisations often reply that maintaining alternatives is expensive. Sometimes that is true, and resources are finite. But the cost comparison should include work displaced onto users and the later costs of unresolved errors. Offering a telephone route for occasional exceptions may be cheaper than rebuilding every digital screen, while clearer instructions may reduce calls. There is no universal requirement to operate every possible channel forever. There is a requirement to examine the consequences of removing a channel instead of treating the savings on one departmental budget as the whole social result.

H. Convenience is best understood as a relationship between a service and a situation, not a permanent property of an interface. A well-designed system can make routine tasks quick, preserve reasonable alternatives and handle unusual cases without humiliation or excessive delay. It should be evaluated with unsuccessful attempts visible, not only completed transactions. The aim is not to celebrate difficulty or resist technology. It is to make the promise of reduced effort honest: an improvement should not be declared complete merely because the people still struggling have disappeared from the measurement.

Caller: It’s Harker, H-A-R-K-E-R. The event is on the nineteenth of October. We originally planned the eighteenth, but the hall was booked, so please use 19 October.
Assistant: I have that. What would you like to hire? We have a large television display or a projector with a separate screen. The display is easier in daylight but more difficult to transport.
Caller: We’ll close the curtains, so a projector should be fine. We don’t need a microphone; there will only be twenty people and the room is small. A projector is the main thing, plus the screen if that’s separate.
Assistant: It is separate, but included in the same community rate. Collection can be on the event day or the afternoon before. If you haven’t used the equipment, I’d recommend the previous day so you can test your files in the hall.
Caller: The previous afternoon works. I finish work at three, so could I collect at four?
Assistant: Yes, 4:00 is fine. Please allow twenty minutes for us to demonstrate the connections. We can’t leave the equipment outside for a quick pickup if you arrive after we close.
Caller: What will the charge be?
Assistant: Twenty-eight pounds for the projector and screen together. The forty-pound rate on one part of the website is for a commercial booking. We’ll also take a refundable security deposit, but the actual hire charge for your group is £28. Bring the booking confirmation so the desk applies the correct category.
---
Caller: My laptop is fairly new. Do I need an extra cable?
Assistant: Bring your laptop for the demonstration and we can check its sockets. We supply the ordinary connection cable, and an adapter if required. Please don’t buy an adapter before we know which one you need; they can look similar but serve different functions.
Caller: Good. What identification do you require? I don’t have a driving licence.
Assistant: A passport is fine. We also need proof of the address used for the booking, but that can be a recent bill. We don’t keep a copy of the passport image, just a record that identification was checked.
Caller: Will the equipment fit in a small car?
Assistant: The projector comes in a padded case. The folded screen is longer and might need the rear seats down. Check the dimensions in the confirmation before travelling. Two people aren’t normally necessary, but don’t force the screen into a space that bends its frame.
Caller: We’ll test it as you suggest. The photographs are in a presentation. Should I rely on the hall’s internet connection for the final few images?
Assistant: I’d save a backup locally, ideally on a memory stick as well as on the laptop. The projector doesn’t supply internet access, and a connection problem shouldn’t stop the whole evening. Check that the files open without needing an online account.

Assistant: Return by ten the next morning. Bring it to the warehouse entrance, which is around the back; collections use the front desk. Staff at the warehouse check all the pieces before releasing the security deposit. If an item is missing, call us rather than making another journey with an incomplete set and hoping nobody notices.

Assistant: Look for the community-group category, and I’ll attach a note confirming the equipment we’ve discussed.

Part 2 · An induction for citizen weather observers

Coordinator: Welcome to the weather-observation project. We are comparing conditions across different parts of the town, and your observations will complement the fixed station at the college. They won’t replace it. A single official site gives a consistent long-term record, while a local network can reveal variation within the town. Please remember that a higher number of observations isn’t useful if the method changes unpredictably from one person to another. Today’s induction explains the details that need to remain consistent.
First, equipment remains the property of the project. It is lent without charge, but please report a fault promptly instead of making an unrecorded replacement. Two instruments sold under the same broad description may behave differently. We can compare a replacement before it goes into use and mark the date of the change. Otherwise a difference caused by equipment might look like a sudden change in your neighbourhood’s weather.
Site selection comes next. Choose somewhere you can reach safely and repeatedly, but don’t assume the easiest windowsill is suitable. Heat from a wall or an outlet can affect a reading. The project officer will visit to agree a position with you. If you later need to move an instrument, contact us first. A temporary building or growing hedge may matter even if the new spot is only a short distance away.
Please make the standard observation at the agreed time, not whenever you happen to remember. If you miss it, record the omission. Don’t enter a plausible-looking number from a phone forecast to fill the gap. A visible missing value is more useful than a hidden mixture of observed and predicted data. You can add a note explaining the problem, which helps us distinguish a forgotten reading from equipment failure.
For severe conditions, your safety comes before a reading. Stay indoors if going out would be dangerous. Nobody should climb over a fallen branch to preserve a perfect attendance record. The analysis will account for missing observations, and the project is not a competition to collect data at any cost.
---
There are five routine records to keep, each with a particular instruction. For the thermometer reading, wait until the instrument has settled after you approach. Don’t hold it in your hand while reading, because your body can influence the result. The project guide explains the short waiting procedure, and it is the same for everyone.
For rainfall, empty the collector after taking the daily reading. Otherwise yesterday’s water can be counted again. If you’ve been away, note the longer collection period rather than dividing the total into invented daily values. We need to know what interval the measurement actually covers.
For cloud observations, use the reference sheet. Its examples help distinguish the categories used in this project. You don’t need to memorise a professional atlas. The aim is consistency in a limited set of observations, not to claim that every complicated sky can be described perfectly by one simple label.
For wind direction, report the direction the wind comes from. This is easy to reverse if you focus on where a flag is pointing away from its support. Practise with the officer during the first visit, and ask if the local buildings make the indication unclear.
Finally, for unusual events, add a photograph where it is safe and practical. A picture of ice or a flooded path can help interpret a short written note. Don’t photograph identifiable neighbours without permission, and don’t enter private land to improve a view. The photo is supporting evidence, not a reason to take a risk.
You will receive a monthly summary showing how your record fits the network. Differences aren’t automatically errors. Part of the purpose is to understand real local variation, while recording enough context to distinguish it from the effects of instruments and methods.

Part 3 · Comparing two audio guides

Tutor: I understand you’re comparing audio guides at the gallery. What is the question?
Alice: Whether a guide told as a short story changes what visitors remember compared with a factual list. We don’t want to assume that a story is necessarily better, just because we find it more entertaining.
Jamal: Both versions will cover the same three paintings. We need to keep the information content comparable, though the organisation will differ.
Tutor: And length? A longer guide could produce more recall simply because it includes more exposure.
Alice: We’ve edited both to about four minutes, read by the same speaker at the same pace. We first used two voices, but that would introduce another difference, so we’ve removed it.
Jamal: We also need to avoid people hearing both versions and recognising repeated facts. We plan separate visitor groups rather than having everyone listen twice.
Tutor: How will you assign them?
Alice: We’ll use a pre-set random list, not let people choose story or list. Otherwise people with different interests might select the version they expect to like, and the groups would already differ.
Jamal: The invitation will say it’s a study of guide formats, without calling one the creative version. We shouldn’t encourage a preference before anyone has heard it.
Tutor: Good. How will you assess memory?
Alice: With a short set of questions after the visit. Some ask for facts from the guide, and one asks visitors to connect a painting with an explanation. We’re not measuring everything they learn in the gallery.
Jamal: We should ask about prior familiarity too. Someone who knew a painting already might answer correctly without relying on either guide.
Tutor: Yes. Record that and explain how you use it in analysis. Be careful not to discard knowledgeable visitors after seeing which condition they were in. Your inclusion rules should be defined before collecting results.
---
Alice: For the practical tasks, the audio files are edited but need a listening trial on the actual devices. They sound clear on our laptops, but we haven’t checked the gallery headsets.
Jamal: We can pilot those tomorrow. The memory questions need tutor approval. We’ve drafted them, but we’d like you to check that none gives away an answer to another.
Tutor: Send them today. I can review the content, but the pilot should also test how long the questionnaire takes. A theoretically good question can still be confusing to a tired visitor standing near the exit.
Alice: The gallery permission is complete. The education officer sent the signed approval this morning, including the times when we can approach visitors.
Jamal: We originally included a question asking visitors to rate the café. It’s unrelated and comes from a template we borrowed, so we’re going to delete it rather than collect information with no clear use.
Tutor: Good. A template is a starting point, not authority to ask every question printed on it.
Alice: The final comparison chart will wait until we have data. We know the variables, but if scores cluster near the maximum we may need a display that shows that clearly, not just two broad average bars.
Jamal: We’ll decide the presentation after looking at the distribution, and explain the choice. We won’t change the research question to make the chart more exciting.
Tutor: That’s the right distinction. Analysis needs a plan, while presentation should remain responsive to the data’s shape. Keep records of decisions so a reader can follow the route from question to conclusion.
Alice: The gallery hopes the story version will work well because it is considering a larger production. We’ll make clear that our small study can inform that decision but cannot guarantee the same effect for every painting or visitor.
Tutor: Exactly. Useful evidence is not the same as a universal promise, and an honest limitation need not make the project unhelpful.

Part 4 · Why museum stores need good information

Lecturer: A museum store is often imagined as a room full of objects waiting to appear in an exhibition. In practice, it is an information system with physical responsibilities. An object that is preserved perfectly but cannot be found is unavailable for research. An object that can be found but has lost its identity may be equally difficult to interpret. Today we’ll follow the basic journey of an item entering a fictional local museum, concentrating on the connection between its physical location and its documentary record.
The museum first establishes ownership. A donation, a loan and an item left temporarily for identification create different obligations. Staff should not assume that possession means permission to display, alter or dispose of an object. The agreement records what has been transferred and which conditions apply. This may sound administrative, but uncertainty here can undermine later decisions, especially when the person who brought the item is no longer available to explain the original conversation. A clear record protects the museum and the people connected with the object.
Each accepted object receives a unique number. That number links the item to its catalogue record, photographs and associated documents. It should not depend on a shelf location, because objects move. A label that says only where an item currently sits becomes misleading when a store is rearranged. Staff use an appropriate marking method that does not damage the material, and detachable parts need a documented relationship to the whole. Otherwise a lid and a container can become two apparently unrelated mysteries after being separated for treatment.
A condition report describes the object’s state at entry. It distinguishes existing damage from changes observed later. Good photographs help, but a photograph alone may not show a loose joint, an unstable surface or a part hidden from view. Staff combine images with written observations and specify which areas could not be inspected. The report should not make an uncertain diagnosis sound definitive. A mark that might be mould requires investigation and precaution, not a confident label added by someone without the relevant expertise.
Storage supports are chosen for the item, rather than forcing every object into identical packaging. A heavy piece may need support across its base; a fragile projection may need space around it. The support should allow safe handling without unnecessary direct contact. Where practical, a tray can move with the object. Shelving must also accommodate retrieval, since packing objects densely can make access hazardous. The apparent efficiency of filling every gap disappears if retrieving one item requires moving several vulnerable neighbours.
Location records must change whenever an object moves. This includes temporary moves to photography, conservation or an educational session, not just permanent transfers between stores. The record identifies who moved it, when and where it is expected to be. A temporary location left undocumented can become a long-term disappearance. Staff therefore check movements as part of ordinary work rather than waiting for an annual inventory to reveal that something is missing. Regular audits test whether the system describes what is actually on the shelves.
The catalogue also contains interpretation: what an object may have been used for, who made it and which evidence supports those claims. New research can revise these accounts. The system should retain a history of changes instead of silently replacing an earlier attribution. A researcher may need to understand why an object was once described differently. Separating observation from interpretation helps too. Dimensions measured directly have a different status from a maker’s name inferred from a resemblance, even when both appear in the same database entry.
Finally, digital records need their own care. Backups should be tested, and access permissions should protect sensitive information without making routine work impossible. A copy that has never been restored offers uncertain protection. The museum also needs a plan for future software changes so that records remain usable when a particular application becomes obsolete. Caring for a collection means caring for the connections that make objects meaningful. The physical store and the catalogue are partners: neither can fulfil the museum’s responsibility while the other is neglected.

passages.title: Reading passage 1 · The unexpected life of a public clock
passages.text:
A. When the clock above Fenwick Hall stopped, few residents knew who was responsible for repairing it. The building belonged to the fictional town council, but the clock mechanism had been maintained for decades by a family of watchmakers. The last watchmaker had retired without a written agreement about future work. A digital display could have told the time more cheaply, yet residents objected to losing the familiar face above the square. The dispute began as a question about one broken object and became a discussion about the knowledge required to keep public things working.

B. The council hired conservator Iris Lane to examine the mechanism before inviting repair bids. She found that some components were original while others had been altered during earlier maintenance. These changes were not all defects. A later winding arrangement had reduced the need to climb the narrow tower stairs, making routine care safer. Lane recommended documenting the layers of work rather than returning everything to an imagined first condition. The clock's history included its repairs. Removing every later addition would erase evidence of how different generations had adapted the object to changing needs.

C. Finding a suitable repairer proved difficult. Several firms could replace the entire mechanism but only one offered to repair the worn gears. The firm asked for detailed measurements and photographs before quoting a price. It also warned that an estimate might change once the mechanism was dismantled. The council published a provisional budget with a contingency rather than announcing a fixed price that depended on parts nobody had yet inspected. Residents could see why uncertainty remained, even though the public discussion had understandably demanded a simple answer to the question of how much repair would cost.

D. Temporary removal of the hands created a chance to examine the clock face. From the pavement, it appeared sound, but close inspection revealed loose fixings behind the numerals. Repairing the visible mechanism alone would have left this separate risk untreated. The team coordinated the work so that scaffolding served both tasks. It also checked the roof above the clock, where a small leak had allowed moisture to reach the housing. Treating the clock as an isolated device would have missed its dependence on the building around it and produced a repair with a shorter life.

E. The watchmaker's notebooks provided clues about earlier faults but contained abbreviations that the repair firm could not initially interpret. The retired craftsman agreed to discuss them in recorded interviews. His explanations included details never written down, such as the sound that indicated a particular bearing needed attention. The council obtained permission to keep the recordings with the maintenance archive. It did not publish his personal correspondence. Preserving useful knowledge did not require treating every document associated with the craftsperson as public property, and he helped decide which materials were relevant to future care.

F. Once repaired, the clock still needed regular checks. Two council technicians trained with the firm and used a shared checklist so that responsibility would not depend on one person. The archive included drawings, parts information and a schedule of observations. A local school visited the workshop to see a removed gear, but students were not permitted to enter the tower while maintenance was under way. Public interest was encouraged within practical limits. The council wanted residents to understand the work without turning a functioning piece of infrastructure into an attraction that interfered with its upkeep.

G. The clock's return prompted debate about accuracy. It occasionally differed slightly from the time shown on phones, leading some residents to call the repair unsuccessful. Lane argued that expectations needed to match the mechanism, while others insisted a public clock should still be useful. The council set an agreed tolerance and a procedure for correction. It did not defend every deviation as charming history. Conservation and service were treated as compatible responsibilities: the object could retain its character while remaining subject to an explicit standard that users and technicians could understand.

H. Fenwick's fictional clock offers a modest lesson about stewardship. Public objects can appear to belong to everyone while their survival depends on responsibilities known to very few. Repairing them requires skills, records, access arrangements and continuing expenditure, not only admiration for their appearance. The project succeeded by making those dependencies visible and giving them an institutional home. Its most important result may not have been the moving hands, but the fact that the next failure would begin with an archive and a named team rather than another search for whoever used to know what to do.

passages.title: Reading passage 2 · Searching for stories in old paper
passages.text:
A. An old sheet of paper carries more than written words. Its fibres, folds, stains and surface marks may preserve evidence of manufacture and use. Historians and conservators examine such features to ask questions a transcription cannot answer: whether two pages came from a similar supply, whether a document was repeatedly folded for travel, or whether a mark was present before writing began. In a fictional investigation of a merchant's archive, a team combined material observation with reading. The object was neither to replace interpretation with laboratory tests nor to treat physical evidence as merely decorative background.

B. Conservator Mira Han first inspected sheets under ordinary and transmitted light. In the second method, light passes through the paper, making differences in thickness easier to see. Some sheets contained a watermark, a design formed during manufacture rather than printed afterwards. Han photographed each mark with a scale and recorded its position. She warned that a similar design did not guarantee an identical date or workshop. Motifs could be copied, equipment could remain in use and sheets could be stored for years. The marks offered relationships to investigate, not a calendar readable without qualification.

C. Historian Oscar Bell examined the written dates and the merchant's account entries. A group of letters bearing the same watermark had been written over a longer period than expected. Bell proposed that the merchant had purchased a large stock of paper, but treated this as a possibility rather than a proven fact. He looked for purchase records and references to stationery in the correspondence. Their absence did not disprove the idea; merchants do not document every ordinary supply decision. It did mean that the material pattern alone could not establish the exact circumstances of acquisition.

D. Imaging specialist Tessa Roy used carefully controlled digital photographs to compare faint features. Adjusting contrast made some marks easier to see, but could also exaggerate irregular shadows. Roy kept original images beside processed versions and recorded the settings used. She opposed displaying an enhanced outline without its underlying photograph, because a clean line could make an uncertain reading look like an observed fact. Two researchers traced the faintest marks independently before comparing them. Disagreement was retained in the catalogue so that later readers could distinguish a shared observation from one person's plausible reconstruction.

E. Materials researcher Pavel Ilic examined fibres from tiny fragments already detached from damaged edges. The team did not cut samples from sound sheets merely to complete the table. Fibre composition could indicate differences between groups, but it could not identify an individual maker with certainty. Ilic compared results with the imaging and written evidence rather than treating the laboratory analysis as a final authority. Where methods suggested different groupings, the team checked its assumptions about reuse and repair. A document could contain an old patch added much later, producing material evidence of more than one moment.

F. Folds offered another line of enquiry. Some letters had patterns consistent with compact packets, while others showed broad storage creases. Yet later filing could alter a sheet, and repeated opening could weaken the same lines. Han recorded wear at intersections rather than inferring a complete journey from one fold. The team found that several apparently unrelated letters shared a distinctive filing pattern. This suggested a period of storage together, though it did not prove they had travelled together. Separating those possibilities helped prevent an attractive story from outrunning the observations on which it rested.

G. The final catalogue included structured fields for measurements and longer notes for unresolved interpretations. A short label such as same paper was replaced with a more precise description of which features matched. This made entries less elegant but more useful to future researchers asking different questions. The archive also retained images that had not contributed to the published argument. Later work might find a significant feature the original team had overlooked. Documentation was intended to preserve opportunities for disagreement, not merely to assemble illustrations supporting a single convincing account of the merchant's activity.

H. The fictional project shows why material history depends on restraint as much as discovery. A watermark, fibre sample or fold can narrow possibilities without selecting one final explanation. Combining evidence helps only when the uncertainties of each source remain visible. The sheet is a witness that cannot answer follow-up questions, and careful methods cannot make it speak more clearly than its condition allows. They can, however, leave a record in which another researcher can see the difference between what was measured, what was inferred and what remains open to a future investigation.

passages.title: Reading passage 3 · What a forecast can promise
passages.text:
A. A forecast is useful because a decision must be made before its outcome is known. The need for action does not disappear when prediction is uncertain; a transport operator still needs a timetable and a farmer still needs to decide when to work. Public disappointment often arises when a forecast is interpreted as a promise rather than a conditional account of what may happen. Improving forecasts therefore involves both technical performance and the way results are connected to decisions. A number can become more precise without becoming more useful if its recipient misunderstands what the number represents.

B. Suppose a fictional town uses a model to estimate the chance that a river will exceed a specified level. A probability is not a fraction of the river that will flood, nor a guarantee that the event will occur on that proportion of the town. It describes uncertainty about a defined event under the available information. The event's definition matters: a small rise above a marker and severe flooding are different outcomes. A message that drops the definition while displaying a prominent percentage can create confidence in an answer to a question nobody actually asked.

C. Forecasts are often judged by whether the most likely outcome occurred. That is useful but incomplete. An event assigned a low probability should still happen occasionally if the system is well calibrated. Calibration concerns whether events assigned similar probabilities occur at corresponding frequencies across many cases. One surprising outcome cannot establish that every forecast was defective. Equally, a sequence of successful predictions of common events may say little about performance on rare events that cause the greatest harm. Evaluation needs to consider the whole pattern of claims rather than celebrating or condemning individual moments.

D. Decision thresholds introduce another complication. Two users can receive the same forecast and reasonably choose different actions because their costs differ. Closing a riverside footpath may be inexpensive compared with evacuating a neighbourhood. An action taken for an event that does not occur is not automatically a mistake: the decision may have been justified by the expected harm and the information available. Judging it only after the outcome is known rewards luck and penalises prudent preparation. Accountability should examine the decision process as well as the eventual state of the river.

E. This argument can be misused to protect poor forecasting from criticism. Claiming uncertainty is not permission to make vague statements that cannot be checked. A forecast should specify its event, time window and relevant conditions well enough to support evaluation. Where estimates change, the reasons for revision should be recorded. New measurements can legitimately alter a prediction; quietly replacing an earlier estimate and presenting the latest one as if it had always been issued cannot. A traceable history allows users to distinguish learning from rewriting the record after the result becomes obvious.

F. Communication should also reflect what recipients can do. A broad warning may be appropriate for an early planning decision, while a later operational choice requires more local detail. Repeating a general probability in every message ignores these differences. People need to know which action is being considered, how much time remains and what further information may arrive. This does not require pretending that uncertainty has disappeared. It requires arranging uncertainty around the practical sequence of decisions, so that information becomes available before the opportunity to act has passed rather than only when confidence is highest.

G. Trust is sometimes imagined as unquestioning acceptance of expert forecasts. A healthier form of trust allows users to understand limits, ask questions and revise expectations. Overstating certainty may secure immediate attention but makes later revision look like incompetence or deception. Honest qualifications can seem less dramatic, yet build a more durable relationship when paired with clear guidance. The forecaster should not transfer all responsibility to the audience through an unreadable list of caveats. Nor should the audience demand certainty that the evidence cannot provide. Both require an account of what can reasonably be known now.

H. The useful promise of a forecast is consequently modest but substantial: to organise current evidence in a way that supports a better decision than unaided guesswork. It cannot guarantee a favourable outcome, and no amount of explanation excuses a model that performs badly. Technical evaluation, transparent revision and decision-focused communication must work together. The test is not whether uncertainty can be removed from public life. It is whether people can act intelligently while acknowledging it, and later learn from the difference between what was expected and what actually happened.
